How to Use This Book

This book is written so that you can prepare the whole of Section B of MTE 4107 without opening the lecture slides. Each chapter follows the same order:

  1. Theory: everything on the KMS slides and handwritten notes, rewritten as exam-ready paragraphs, tables and diagrams, plus the standard theory the past papers need but the slides omit.
  2. Derivations: every formula used in an answer is derived step by step (ζ from overshoot, Routh array, Kalman gain, AHP consistency, road-load power, step-climbing condition).
  3. Solved past questions: every Section B question of the 2022, 2023 and 2024 term finals, quoted word for word with year, number and marks, and answered at the length the marks call for.
  4. Checks: every numerical answer was recomputed in Python; the plots are generated from the same calculations.

The theory follows the KMS lecture material for MTE 4107: L1 Sensor modeling (pptx), MTE4107 L2 Actuator and Drive Systems (pdf of the pptx; the pptx and pdf have the same 40 pages/slides, and the pdf page numbers are cited), L3 Control System design, L4 Performance Indices, L9 Data Acquisition and Control, L10 I/O, L11 Data Communication & Network, and the handwritten notes lead lag v3 and optimization kms (image-only; read page by page). The 30° climb (a 58 % grade) needs 155 kW (average, accelerating) and 266 kW (75 mph) – more than any listed motor, even two HPD 40s; this is stated in the answer rather than hidden. Acceleration power is sized on the average (energy) basis; one HPD 40 at 1:1 gearing is torque-limited to ≈ 12 s for 0–60 mph, so two units are recommended for the 6 s target.

1. The Mechatronic Design Process, Embedded Design and Optimization ★★★

A mechatronic system is a synergistic combination of mechanical engineering, electronics, control engineering and computer software, designed together so that the whole performs better than the parts designed separately. A washing machine, an anti-lock braking system, a CNC machine, a robot arm, an autonomous mobile robot and a myoelectric prosthetic hand are all mechatronic systems: each senses its environment, decides in a processor, and acts through actuators on a mechanical structure. This chapter covers how such a system is designed, the role of documentation, the design of the embedded controller and the role of optimization, which together form the "Introduction" and "Integration and Optimization" parts of the syllabus.

1.1 Structure of a Mechatronic System

Every mechatronic system contains the same functional elements, whatever its size:

ElementFunctionExamples
Mechanical systemStructure, mechanisms and transmissions that carry loads and produce the useful motionframe, linkages, gears, belts, bearings, wheels
SensorsConvert physical quantities (position, speed, force, temperature) into electrical signalsencoder, IMU, load cell, EMG electrode
Signal conditioning and interfacingAmplify, filter, isolate and digitise sensor signals; drive actuators from logic-level commandsinstrumentation amplifier, ADC, H-bridge
Controller (processor)Runs the control algorithm and decision logicmicrocontroller, PLC, PC, DSP, FPGA
ActuatorsConvert electrical, hydraulic or pneumatic energy into controlled motionDC/servo/stepper motor, cylinder, solenoid
SoftwareControl laws, state machines, communication, user interface, diagnosticsfirmware, RTOS, HMI
Power supplyProvides energy to every subsystembattery, SMPS, compressor
Integrated design: the key idea
In traditional (sequential) design the mechanical engineer designs the machine, then the electrical engineer adds drives, then the control engineer tries to make it work. In mechatronic (concurrent) design all disciplines work on one shared model from the start, so that trade-offs are made at system level: a lighter, more flexible arm can be accepted if the controller compensates for its vibration; a cheaper sensor can be used if software filtering removes its noise. The integration issues are interfaces (mechanical–electrical, analog–digital), timing, noise and EMC, power, heat, and the reliability of the whole.

1.2 The Mechatronic Design Process

The design of a mechatronic product follows a sequence of stages with feedback between them (Fig. 1.1).

  1. Recognition of the need. A customer, market or social need is identified and written as a problem statement: what the machine must do, for whom, in what environment and at what cost.
  2. Conceptual design and functional specification. The required functions are listed (e.g. "grip objects of 0–2 kg", "move at 0.5 m/s"), and quantitative targets are fixed: loads, speeds, accuracy, response time, power, size, mass, cost, safety standards. Several concepts are generated and compared (morphological chart, weighted decision matrix).
  3. First-principle modular design. The chosen concept is divided into modules (mechanical structure, sensors, actuators and drives, controller hardware, software), each with defined interfaces.
  4. Modelling and simulation. Mathematical models (transfer functions, state space, finite element, circuit models) predict behaviour before hardware is built.
  5. Optimization. Design variables (gear ratio, link lengths, controller gains, motor size) are tuned to minimise cost, mass or error subject to constraints (§1.5).
  6. Integration of modules. Mechanical, electrical, control and software parts are combined; interface problems (noise, timing, mounting) appear here.
  7. Prototyping and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation. The real controller is tested against a real-time simulated plant, then a physical prototype is built.
  8. Testing and validation. The prototype is tested against every requirement in the specification. Failures send the design back to an earlier stage.
  9. Design documentation, production and service. Drawings, schematics, code, test reports and manuals are finalised for manufacture and maintenance.

1.3 Embedded System Design with a Microcontroller

An embedded system is a computer system dedicated to one function inside a larger machine (the controller of a washing machine, the ECU of an ABS, the processor of a prosthetic hand). It must meet real-time deadlines, run on limited power and memory, and survive the machine's environment. The KMS lecture on control system design lists the physical controllers from which the designer chooses:

ControllerAdvantagesLimitationsTypical use
Microcontroller (PIC, Arduino; Raspberry Pi is a microprocessor board)Compact, light, low power; cheap in volume; programmed in high-level languagesLimited I/O and processing power; needs extra hardware; sensitive to EMI; large design effortHousehold appliances, automotive modules, low-cost embedded systems
PLCProtected (opto-isolated) I/O; immune to EMI and harsh environments; modular; ladder logic; PID and communication add-onsLarger and dearer; limited signal processing; slow for high-speed real timeIndustrial automation, process control
PC (desktop/laptop)Excellent user interface and computing power; rapid prototypingCostly, bulky; not for dusty sites; OS not real-time; needs I/O cardsR&D, laboratory automation
PACPLC robustness with PC software flexibility; real-timeCostModern automation with data processing
DSP chipVery fast numerical computation (filters, FFT)Specialised programmingMotor control, vibration analysis, audio
FPGA / PLD / logic gatesVery high speed, parallel, reliableVHDL/Verilog, complex designHigh-speed digital control, robotics
RelaysSimple ON/OFF logicBulky, slow, contact wear, high powerLargely obsolete

The microcontroller is the usual choice for a compact, battery-powered, mass-produced mechatronic product. Its design follows the steps answered in §1.10.

1.4 Why Requirements Come First

A design can only be judged against what it is supposed to do. The requirements specification is the reference for every later decision: it fixes the loads (which size the actuators and structure), the speeds and accuracies (which select sensors, controller and sample rate), the environment (which fixes sealing, temperature range and EMC measures) and the cost. A requirement that is discovered late forces rework of every module built on the old assumption, and the cost of a change rises steeply as the design moves from paper to prototype to production. This is answered fully in §1.8.

1.5 Optimization in Mechatronic Design

Optimization is the process of finding the values of the design variables that give the best value of a chosen measure of merit (minimum cost, mass, energy or error; maximum efficiency or speed) while satisfying all the constraints. Every optimization problem has the same parts:

Standard form of an optimization problem
Minimise f(X),X=(x1,x2,…,xn)T  (design variables)subject to gj(X)≤0, j=1,…,J  (inequality constraints)subject to hk(X)=0, k=1,…,K  (equality constraints)subject to xi(L)≤xi≤xi(U)  (variable bounds)\begin{aligned}&\text{Minimise } f(\mathbf X),\qquad \mathbf X=(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n)^T\ \ \text{(design variables)}\\&\text{subject to } g_j(\mathbf X)\le0,\ j=1,\dots,J\ \ \text{(inequality constraints)}\\&\phantom{\text{subject to }}h_k(\mathbf X)=0,\ k=1,\dots,K\ \ \text{(equality constraints)}\\&\phantom{\text{subject to }}x_i^{(L)}\le x_i\le x_i^{(U)}\ \ \text{(variable bounds)}\end{aligned}​Minimise f(X),X=(x1​,x2​,…,xn​)T  (design variables)subject to gj​(X)≤0, j=1,…,J  (inequality constraints)subject to hk​(X)=0, k=1,…,K  (equality constraints)subject to xi(L)​≤xi​≤xi(U)​  (variable bounds)​ Maximising FFF is the same as minimising −F-F−F.
Conditions for an optimum (KMS optimization notes)
Necessary condition: at an interior optimum the first derivative (gradient) is zero, f′(x∗)=0f'(x^*)=0f′(x∗)=0 or ∇f(X∗)=0\nabla f(\mathbf X^*)=\mathbf 0∇f(X∗)=0.
Sufficient condition: one variable: f′′(x∗)>0f''(x^*)>0f′′(x∗)>0 ⇒ local minimum, f′′(x∗)<0f''(x^*)<0f′′(x∗)<0 ⇒ local maximum. Several variables: the Hessian H=[∂2f/∂xi∂xj]\mathbf H=[\partial^2f/\partial x_i\partial x_j]H=[∂2f/∂xi​∂xj​] positive definite (all leading principal minors >0>0>0) ⇒ local minimum; negative definite ⇒ maximum; indefinite ⇒ saddle point.
Equality constraint: eliminate a variable by substitution, or use a Lagrange multiplier L=f+λhL=f+\lambda hL=f+λh. Inequality constraint: Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions: ∇f+λ∇g=0\nabla f+\lambda\nabla g=0∇f+λ∇g=0, g≤0g\le0g≤0, λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0, λg=0\lambda g=0λg=0. For a convex problem (convex objective, convex constraints) these conditions are necessary and sufficient.

Worked lecture example: open-topped box of minimum surface area

Find the dimensions that minimise the surface area of an open-topped rectangular box of volume V=972 m3V=972\ \text{m}^3V=972 m3 whose bottom is twice as long as it is wide.

Step 1 — design variables: width www, length lll, height hhh.

Step 2 — constraints: wlh=972wlh=972wlh=972 and l=2wl=2wl=2w. They are equalities, so use them to eliminate variables: h=972w(2w)=486w2h=\dfrac{972}{w(2w)}=\dfrac{486}{w^2}h=w(2w)972​=w2486​.

Step 3 — objective: area of bottom plus four sides (no top):

1.6 Past Question: Why Optimization Is Necessary

2023 · Q5(a)Why optimization is necessary in mechatronics system design? Explain with example.10Topic: need for optimization

A mechatronic system combines mechanical, electrical, electronic, control and software subsystems whose design decisions are coupled and often in conflict. Optimization is the systematic way to find the best compromise instead of settling for the first design that works. It is necessary because:

  1. Subsystems are coupled. A larger motor gives more torque but adds mass and inertia, which needs more torque, a bigger drive and a bigger battery. Only a system-level optimization balances all of these at once.
  2. Requirements conflict. Speed against accuracy, stiffness against weight, performance against cost, fast response against overshoot and actuator saturation. Optimization picks the best trade-off and makes it explicit.
  3. Hard constraints must be respected. Current and thermal limits, stress, space envelope, standards and actuator saturation define a feasible region; optimization finds the best design that provably lies inside it.
  4. Competitiveness. Small savings in cost, energy or mass are multiplied over every unit produced; a lighter robot arm moves faster with the same motors.
  5. Controller tuning. The best gains are those that minimise a performance index (ISE, ITAE, quadratic cost) – an optimization problem by definition (Chapter 6).
  6. Fewer prototypes. Optimising a model before building hardware reduces design–build–test cycles, development time and cost.
Example 1: PI controller under actuator saturation (KMS notes)
Minimising the tracking cost alone gives kp=4k_p=4kp​=4, ki=2k_i=2ki​=2, but then kp+2ki=8k_p+2k_i=8kp​+2ki​=8 exceeds the actuator limit 6, so the real actuator saturates and the response is poor. Constrained optimization (Lagrange/KKT) gives kp=3.2k_p=3.2kp​=3.2, ki=1.4k_i=1.4ki​=1.4, the best gains the hardware can actually deliver.
Example 2: gear ratio for a servo drive
A motor of inertia JmJ_mJm​ drives a load JLJ_LJL​ through a gear ratio nnn. The load acceleration is αL=nTmn2Jm+JL\alpha_L=\dfrac{nT_m}{n^2J_m+J_L}αL​=n2Jm​+JL​nTm​​. A small nnn gives little torque multiplication; a large nnn makes the reflected motor inertia n2Jmn^2J_mn2Jm​ dominate. Setting dαL/dn=0d\alpha_L/dn=0dαL​/dn=0 gives the optimum n∗=JL/Jmn^*=\sqrt{J_L/J_m}n∗=JL​/Jm​​ (inertia matching). Guessing nnn wastes motor capacity.

Other examples: minimum-mass robot links subject to a deflection limit; minimum-energy trajectory for a battery robot; sensor placement for maximum observability; the open box of §1.5.

1.7 Past Question: Optimal Design Flowchart, Design Variables and Constraints

2023 · Q5(b)Draw a flow chart of optimal design procedure. How design variables and constraints are selected in optimization problem?13Topic: formulation of an optimal design problem

The procedure starts by recognising the need for optimization. The designer then chooses the design variables, formulates the constraints and the objective function, and sets the variable bounds. A suitable algorithm is then chosen (analytical for small smooth problems; numerical or non-traditional, e.g. genetic algorithm, for large or non-smooth ones) and the optimal solution is obtained. If the solution is unsatisfactory – it lies on a bound, violates an un-modelled requirement or is not practical – the formulation is revised and the loop repeats.

Selection of design variables

  1. List all parameters of the design. Those that strongly affect performance and can be changed by the designer become design variables; the rest are fixed parameters.
  2. The choice depends on the objective: a parameter that dominates cost may be irrelevant to life or accuracy.
  3. Choose as few as possible, because the effort of every algorithm grows rapidly with the number of variables; start with the most sensitive ones.
  4. Choose independent variables; eliminate dependent ones through equality relations (in the box example h=486/w2h=486/w^2h=486/w2 removed hhh and l=2wl=2wl=2w removed lll).
  5. In mechatronics typical variables are dimensions, gear ratio, motor size, spring stiffness and controller gains.

Selection of constraints

  1. Identify the physical laws and resource limits that make a design unacceptable: stress, deflection, buckling, natural frequency, temperature, current, actuator saturation, space, mass and cost.
  2. Write each as a functional relationship among the design variables, e.g. σ(X)≤Sallow\sigma(\mathbf X)\le S_{allow}σ(X)≤Sallow​, kp+2ki≤6k_p+2k_i\le6kp​+2ki​≤6.
  3. Prefer inequality constraints (most engineering limits are of this type); a "≥" constraint becomes "≤" on multiplying by −1, giving the standard form g(X)≤0g(\mathbf X)\le0g(X)≤0.
  4. Keep equality constraints to a minimum: eliminate them by substitution, or relax them into two inequalities (e.g. deflection =5=5=5 mm → 4≤δ≤64\le\delta\le64≤δ≤6 mm) so that algorithms run smoothly.
  5. Distinguish behaviour constraints (limits on performance, e.g. overshoot ≤ 10 %) from side constraints/bounds (limits on the variables themselves, e.g. 4≤d≤144\le d\le144≤d≤14 cm, gains ≥ 0).
  6. Normalise the constraints and check that the feasible region is not empty.
Source lectureKMS · Optimization notes (optimization kms.pdf, pp. 1–3) — Design variables, constraints and objective shown on the box example; the flowchart is not in the notes — see §1.7

1.8 Past Question: Knowing What the Machine Must Do

2023 · Q6(d)Why is it important to know what you want your machine to do before designing it?08Topic: requirements definition

Defining the function and performance of the machine first (the requirements specification) is the foundation of the whole design process:

  1. It sets the design targets. Load, speed, stroke, accuracy, response time and environment fix the size of every component. The KMS drive-system design procedure starts with exactly this step: "define motion requirements – what the system must do (speed, torque, stroke, accuracy, environment)".
  2. It guides component selection. Actuators, sensors, controller and power supply are chosen by comparing their ratings with the requirements; without numbers there is no basis for choosing a 40 kW or a 120 kW motor, a stepper or a servo.
  3. It avoids over- and under-design. An over-designed machine is heavy and expensive; an under-designed one fails in service. Both are wasteful.
  4. It prevents costly rework. A requirement discovered after the mechanical design is frozen may force a new motor, a new drive and a new controller. The cost of a change rises steeply from concept to prototype to production.
  5. It allows integrated design. Mechanical, electrical and software teams work to the same specification, so their modules fit together.
  6. It defines the tests. Validation means checking the prototype against the requirements; vague requirements cannot be verified.
  7. It fixes cost, time and safety limits early, so that trade-offs are made consciously.

Example: a line-following robot that must carry 5 kg at 0.5 m/s on a factory floor needs a different motor, battery and chassis from one that must climb a 15° ramp outdoors; designing before deciding which one is wanted guarantees rework.

Source lectureKMS · L2 – Actuator and Drive Systems (MTE4107 L2 Actuator and Drive Systems.pptx.pdf, p. 40); L2 – Actuator and Drive Systems (MTE4107 L2 Actuator and Drive Systems.pptx.pdf, pp. 7–8) — Only the first design step ("define motion requirements") is given — see §1.8

1.9 Past Question: Documentation in the Design Process

2023 · Q8(a)How important is documentation in each stage of the mechatronics design process?08Topic: design documentation

Documentation is the written record of what was decided, why, and how it was verified. In a multidisciplinary mechatronic project it is the only reliable way to keep the mechanical, electrical and software teams consistent. Its role at each stage:

StageDocuments producedWhy it matters
Recognition of needProblem statement, customer requirementsAgreed goal; basis for all later decisions
Conceptual design / specificationRequirements specification, concept sketches, decision matricesRecords why one concept was chosen; prevents re-arguing decisions
Modular design & modellingCAD drawings, schematics, block diagrams, models, calculations, interface definitionsEach team builds to the same interfaces; calculations can be checked
Component selectionDatasheets, bill of materials, sizing calculationsTraceable choices; spares and alternatives can be found later
Software developmentFlowcharts, state diagrams, commented code, version historyOthers can debug and extend the code; changes can be reverted
Integration & testingTest plans, test results, bug and change logsProves each requirement is met; reveals recurring faults
Production & serviceAssembly instructions, user and maintenance manuals, safety certificatesCorrect manufacture, safe operation, repair and legal compliance

Overall importance: (i) communication among disciplines and with the customer; (ii) traceability of every design decision to a requirement; (iii) continuity when team members change; (iv) easier troubleshooting, maintenance and upgrades; (v) evidence for quality standards, certification, patents and liability; (vi) a knowledge base for future projects. Poor documentation is a common reason why a working prototype cannot be reproduced or maintained.

Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §1.9 of this book)

1.10 Past Question: Steps in Designing an Embedded System

2024 · Q7(c)Briefly explain the steps involved in designing the embedded system.09Topic: embedded system design with microcontroller
  1. Requirements analysis: functions, inputs/outputs, timing deadlines (real-time), accuracy, power budget, size, environment, cost and safety.
  2. System specification: turn the requirements into measurable figures – number and type of I/O channels, sample rates, communication interfaces (UART, I²C, SPI, CAN), memory, supply voltage.
  3. Architecture and hardware/software partitioning: block diagram of the system; decide which functions are done in hardware (filters, PWM generation, encoders) and which in software; single loop, interrupt-driven or RTOS structure.
  4. Component selection: choose the processor (microcontroller, DSP, FPGA – §1.3) with enough speed, memory, ADC channels, timers and peripherals; choose sensors, drivers, regulators and connectors.
  5. Hardware design: schematic (power supply, reset, clock, signal conditioning, protection, drivers), PCB layout with attention to grounding and EMC, prototype board.
  6. Firmware design: device drivers, control algorithm, state machine, communication, fault handling; written in C/C++ and tested on simulators or development boards.
  7. Integration: load the firmware into the target hardware and bring up the subsystems one by one.
  8. Testing, debugging and validation: unit tests, hardware-in-the-loop tests, timing and power measurement, environmental and EMC tests against the specification; return to earlier steps if a requirement is not met.
  9. Deployment and maintenance: production programming, documentation, field updates (bootloader / OTA) and support.
Source lectureKMS · L3 – Control System Design (MTE4107 L3 Control System design.pptx.pdf, pp. 5–10) — Physical controllers only; the design steps are not in the slides — see §1.10

2. Sensors, Signal Conditioning and Op-Amp Circuits ★★★

The syllabus item "Electrical and electronic system design" starts with sensor modelling, sensor selection and signal conditioning and with the "important electronic circuits for mechatronic systems". This chapter teaches the sensor performance terms, how a sensor is selected, what each signal-conditioning block does, the operational-amplifier circuits used to build them, and the special case of the muscle (EMG) sensor used in prosthetic arms.

2.1 Sensors, Transducers and Smart Sensors

A sensor is an element that produces a signal related to the quantity being measured (the measurand). A resistance thermometer, for example, turns a temperature into a change of resistance. A transducer converts energy from one form into another; a sensor is the transducer at the input of a measurement system. Some sensors are packaged with their signal conditioning. When a microprocessor is added in the same package the device is a smart sensor. It can compensate for random errors, adapt to environmental changes, calculate its own accuracy, linearise its output, self-calibrate and diagnose its own faults.

2.2 Performance Terms of a Sensor

TermMeaning
Range, spanRange: the limits between which the input may vary for correct operation (e.g. 0–1000 kPa). Span: the difference of the limits (1000 kPa). Outside the range the sensor saturates or is damaged.
ErrorMeasured value − true value at a given reading.
AccuracyCloseness to the true value considering all error sources; often given as % of full-scale output (FSO). ±5 % FSO on a 0–200 °C sensor means up to ±10 °C anywhere in the range.
SensitivityOutput change ÷ input change (e.g. mV/°C). Sensitivity to unwanted quantities (ambient temperature, supply voltage) causes errors.
Hysteresis errorDifferent outputs for the same input when it is approached increasing and decreasing; the maximum difference is the hysteresis error (friction, magnetism).
Non-linearity errorDeviation of the input–output curve from the ideal straight line.
RepeatabilityAbility to give the same output for the same input repeatedly under the same conditions.
Stability, driftAbility to keep the same output for a constant input over time; a slow change is drift; zero drift is the change of output at zero input.
Dead band, dead timeDead band: range of input with no output change. Dead time: delay between applying the input and the start of the output response.
ResolutionSmallest input change that gives a noticeable output change.

2.3 Sensor Selection

Selection has two stages: (1) choose the type of sensing principle from the measurand and the environment, and (2) choose the specific model from its performance figures. The criteria taught in the KMS lectures are:

  • Measurement requirements: measurand, range and span, accuracy and resolution, sensitivity.
  • Dynamic characteristics: response time, frequency response and bandwidth, damping and lag (lag inside a feedback loop can cause instability).
  • Environment: temperature range, humidity and dust (IP rating, IP65 or higher outdoors), vibration and shock, EMI/EMC.
  • Electrical interface: output type (voltage, current, PWM, I²C, SPI, CAN, RS-485), output impedance and loading, supply, need for external conditioning.
  • Calibration and linearity, reliability: low non-linearity and hysteresis, calibration stability, repeatability, MTBF.
  • Physical constraints and cost: size, weight, mounting, wiring; total cost of ownership, availability of spares, ease of replacement.
  • Smart features: self-diagnostics, fieldbus/IoT protocols, on-board filtering and linearisation.
  • Application-specific needs: robotics (light, high resolution, fast), automotive (temperature, ruggedness, EMI), biomedical (biocompatible, safe, sensitive to small physiological signals), aerospace (precision, low drift).

2.4 Signal Conditioning

Signal conditioning prepares the raw sensor signal so that it can be read correctly by a controller, PLC or data acquisition system. Sensor outputs are often tiny (millivolts from a thermocouple or bridge), noisy, non-linear or in an awkward form (resistance change, charge). The conditioning circuit turns them into a clean, amplified, standard signal: 0–5 V, 0–10 V, 4–20 mA or a digital word.

BlockPurpose
AmplifierRaise low-level signals to the ADC range to use its full resolution; instrumentation and differential amplifiers reject common-mode noise. Place close to the sensor.
FilterRemove unwanted frequencies: low-pass for high-frequency noise (and anti-aliasing before the ADC), high-pass for drift and DC offset, band-pass, notch for 50 Hz mains hum.
IsolatorBreak the electrical connection (optical, magnetic or capacitive coupling) to protect the computer from high voltage spikes, remove ground loops and ensure safety (medical equipment).
ExcitationSupply the stable voltage or current that passive sensors need (strain gauges, RTDs, thermistors); bridge completion.
ADCConvert the conditioned analog signal into digital data.
LinearizerCorrect non-linear sensors (thermocouples, thermistors) in hardware or by software look-up tables or equations.
CompensationCorrect for temperature and other environmental effects (e.g. cold-junction compensation).

Smart/programmable conditioning adds auto-calibration of gain, offset and drift; DSP-based digital filtering; programmable gain; self-diagnostics (broken wire, overload); high-CMRR isolation amplifiers; microcontrollers with Ethernet, CAN or RS-485 output; and wireless modules for IoT sensing.

2.5 Operational-Amplifier Circuits

An ideal op-amp has infinite open-loop gain, infinite input resistance and zero output resistance. With negative feedback two rules follow: (i) no current enters either input; (ii) the two input voltages are equal, V−=V+V_-=V_+V−​=V+​ (virtual short).

CircuitOutputUse

2.6 Past Question: Selecting a Signal-Conditioning System

2024 · Q8(a)Discuss the key factors that must be considered when selecting a signal conditioning system.08Topic: signal-conditioning selection

The right conditioner depends on the sensor, the application and the measurement environment. The key factors are:

  1. Type of sensor and its output. Voltage-output sensors (potentiometer, accelerometer) need voltage amplifiers; current-output sensors (4–20 mA transmitters) may need only isolation or scaling (a precision resistor); resistance-based sensors (RTDs, strain gauges) need excitation and a bridge circuit; thermocouples need cold-junction compensation and linearisation.
  2. Range of the input signal. The gain and input range must match µV, mV or V signals, so that the signal fills the ADC range without saturating.
  3. Required output format. Analog (0–5 V, 0–10 V, 4–20 mA) or digital (RS-485, CAN, USB), as required by the next stage.
  4. Accuracy and resolution. Low noise, low offset and drift, high stability and high CMRR so that the conditioner does not add more error than the sensor.
  5. Environmental conditions. Industrial plants need isolation and shielding against EMI and ground loops; hot areas need thermally stable components.
  6. Dynamic response. Rapidly changing signals (vibration, sound, EMG) need enough bandwidth, and the anti-aliasing filter must suit the sampling rate.
  7. Power and excitation requirements. A stable, suitable excitation voltage or current for the sensor; available supply for the conditioner.
  8. Integration compatibility. Match the output to the DAQ, PLC or microcontroller input range, connectors and software; also cost, size, channel count and smart features (auto-calibration, diagnostics).
Source lectureKMS · L1 – Sensor Modeling (L1Sensor modeling.pptx, slides 21–22)

2.7 Past Question: Conditioning the Muscle (EMG) Signal

2022 · Q7(c)Briefly explain about signal conditioning required to process a signal from muscle sensor employed in prosthetic arm.13Topic: EMG signal conditioning

A myoelectric prosthesis is controlled by the surface electromyogram (sEMG): the electrical activity of the muscles of the residual limb, picked up by electrodes on the skin. The raw signal is very difficult to use directly:

  • amplitude only about 10 µV – 5 mV; useful energy in about 20–500 Hz (most in 50–150 Hz);
  • it is random (noise-like); the information is in its amplitude envelope, which rises with contraction strength;
  • it is contaminated by 50 Hz mains interference (common-mode, often much larger than the EMG), motion artefacts and baseline drift below about 10–20 Hz, a DC electrode–skin offset of up to hundreds of mV, and crosstalk from neighbouring muscles.

The required conditioning stages are:

  1. Electrodes and differential pick-up. Two active electrodes over the muscle and a reference electrode on a bony site. The signal is taken differentially, so interference common to both electrodes cancels. Active electrodes with a buffer at the skin reduce cable noise.
  2. Instrumentation amplifier (pre-amplifier). Very high input impedance (> 10 MΩ, so the skin–electrode impedance does not load the source) and high CMRR (> 90–100 dB) to reject 50 Hz hum. A modest first-stage gain (about 10) keeps the electrode DC offset from saturating it.
  3. High-pass filter (10–20 Hz). Removes the DC offset, baseline drift and motion artefacts.
  4. Notch filter (50 Hz) where residual mains hum remains (optional when CMRR is high, because it also removes some EMG).
  5. Low-pass filter (≈ 450–500 Hz) removes high-frequency noise and acts as the anti-aliasing filter; the ADC must then sample at ≥ 1 kHz (Nyquist).
  6. Main gain stage brings the total gain to about 1000–5000, so the signal fills the ADC range (e.g. 0–3.3 V or 0–5 V).
  7. Full-wave rectification. The EMG swings positive and negative about zero; taking its absolute value (precision rectifier) gives a signal whose mean follows muscle activity.
  8. Envelope detection (smoothing). A low-pass filter of about 2–6 Hz (or an RMS converter / moving average) turns the rectified signal into a smooth envelope proportional to contraction force. This is the control signal: a level above threshold opens or closes the hand, and its height sets speed or grip force (proportional control).
  9. Level shifting, isolation and protection. Offset to a single-supply ADC range; patient isolation and current limiting for safety (the subject is electrically connected to the circuit); ESD protection.
  10. Digitisation and digital processing. The microcontroller ADC samples the signal(s); software computes features (mean absolute value, RMS, zero crossings, waveform length) in windows of about 100–250 ms and uses a threshold or a pattern-recognition classifier (LDA, SVM, neural network) to decide the intended gesture.
Typical numbers to quote
Input 0.1–5 mV; CMRR ≥ 100 dB; input impedance ≥ 10 MΩ; band 20–450 Hz; notch 50 Hz; total gain ≈ 1000; envelope LPF 2–6 Hz; sample rate ≥ 1 kHz; 10–12-bit ADC.
Source lectureKMS · L1 – Sensor Modeling (L1Sensor modeling.pptx, slides 17–19); L9 – Data Acquisition and Control (MTE4107 L9 Data Acquisition and Control.pdf, pp. 8–10) — General signal conditioning only; EMG-specific stages — see §2.7

3. Actuator Selection ★★★

Actuators are the "muscles" of a mechatronic system. They decide how fast, how strong and how precise the machine can be, and they are often its most expensive components. This chapter follows the first half of the KMS lecture Actuator and Drive Systems: what an actuator is, its conversion principle, the selection criteria, the challenges of selection, the subtractive approach, and the weighting and Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) methods used to make the final choice.

3.1 Actuators and the Actuator System

An actuator is an energy converter that transforms energy from an external source into mechanical energy in a controllable way. Its input quantity depends on the type of energy: current, charge or voltage for electromagnetic, piezoelectric and magnetostrictive actuators; pressure or flow for fluid-power actuators; temperature for shape-memory-alloy and thermal-expansion actuators.

  1. Power source – provides the energy (in industry usually electrical or fluid power).
  2. Power converter – supplies (or returns) energy from the source to the actuator according to the controller's orders, e.g. an electrical inverter or a hydraulic proportional valve.
  3. Actuator – converts the source energy into mechanical energy.
  4. Mechanical load – the mechanical system being driven (with its transmission).
  5. Controller – makes the whole system follow the reference set points given by the operator.
  6. Sensors and control algorithm – the controller achieves this by sensing the critical quantities and applying appropriate control algorithms.

3.2 The Actuator (Conversion) Principle

The conversion principle is the physical effect that lets the device turn input energy into motion. It fixes what the actuator can do:

PrinciplePhysical effectCharacteristicsExamples
ElectromagneticForce on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field; magnetic attractionContinuous rotation, wide speed range, excellent controllability, moderate force densityDC, BLDC, stepper, servo motors, solenoids, voice coils
Hydraulic (fluid power)Pressure of an incompressible oil on a piston or vaneVery high force and power density, stiff, needs pump and oil; leaksCylinders, hydraulic motors (excavators, presses)
PneumaticPressure of compressed airClean, cheap, fast, compliant; poor position control (air is compressible)Cylinders, grippers, air muscles
PiezoelectricCrystal strains when a voltage is appliedNanometre resolution, very fast, very small stroke, high voltageNano-positioners, inkjet heads
MagnetostrictiveMaterial strains in a magnetic fieldLarge force, small stroke, high frequencySonar, vibration actuators
Shape-memory alloyPhase change of NiTi on heatingHigh force/weight, silent, slow, low efficiencyMicro-grippers, prosthetic fingers
Thermal expansionMaterials expand when heatedSimple, slow, small displacementBimetallic strips, thermostats

3.3 Why Actuator Selection Matters

Because actuators directly affect system speed, accuracy and reliability, their selection is a critical design task. The choice determines: the performance (speed, precision and torque/force capability); the efficiency and energy consumption; the maintenance requirements and lifetime; and the overall cost of production and operation. Even though actuators are common components, they are among the most critical elements of automation design.

3.4 Actuator Selection Criteria

No actuator type is ideal for all applications, so selection uses several quantitative and qualitative criteria, grouped as functional, environmental and economic:

CriterionWhat is checked
Range of motionLinear stroke or rotary angle needed. Acts as the first filter: pneumatic gives short-to-moderate strokes, hydraulic long strokes with high force, electric linear or rotary.
Available power supplyCompressed air, hydraulic pressure or electricity (AC/DC) already on site; voltage, current and capacity; cost of adding a compressor or pump.
Load characteristicsStatic and dynamic load over the whole cycle; constant, varying, intermittent or shock loads; inertia; holding against gravity; frequent reversal.
ControllabilityEase and accuracy of controlling position, speed, force: electric excellent; hydraulic good over a wide power range; pneumatic limited (on–off tasks).
Directional requirementUnidirectional or bidirectional motion (single- or double-acting).
Noise and thermal emissionSound, vibration and heat produced; operator comfort and reliability.
EnvironmentTemperature, humidity, dust, vibration, corrosion, cleanliness (food, medical), explosion risk.
Speed variationRange of speed adjustment and stability of speed under load or supply changes.
Speed and torque (force)Required torque at the required speed; torque–speed curve must cover the load.
OtherPurchase cost, size and weight.

3.5 Evaluation and Weighting Method

  1. List all relevant criteria.
  2. Give each criterion a weight (importance factor), the weights summing to 1.
  3. Score each actuator type on each criterion (e.g. 1–5).
  4. Multiply weight × score and sum for each actuator.
  5. The highest total indicates the most suitable option.

Weights come from expert judgement (e.g. precision 0.3, cost 0.1 for a precision task) or from pairwise comparison (AHP). Lecture example:

CriterionWeightPneumaticHydraulicElectric
Force capacity0.25253
Precision0.25235
Cost0.20532
Maintenance0.15424
Environment fit0.15534
Total1.003.353.353.60

e.g. electric: 0.25(3)+0.25(5)+0.20(2)+0.15(4)+0.15(4)=0.75+1.25+0.40+0.60+0.60=3.600.25(3)+0.25(5)+0.20(2)+0.15(4)+0.15(4)=0.75+1.25+0.40+0.60+0.60=3.600.25(3)+0.25(5)+0.20(2)+0.15(4)+0.15(4)=0.75+1.25+0.40+0.60+0.60=3.60 → electric actuator chosen.

3.6 The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)

AHP (Saaty) turns many simple pairwise judgements into consistent numerical weights. The criteria are first compared among themselves; then, for each criterion, the alternatives are compared (or rated).

3.7 DC, Stepper and Servo Motors

Brushed DC motor: torque T=KtiT=K_tiT=Kt​i, back-emf e=Keωe=K_e\omegae=Ke​ω; speed set by voltage (PWM), torque by current; simple and cheap but brushes wear. Stepper motor: rotates by a fixed step angle (e.g. 1.8°, 200 steps/rev) per input pulse; position = number of pulses, speed = pulse rate; open loop, holds position, but loses steps if overloaded and resonates. Servo motor: a DC/BLDC/AC motor with a feedback sensor (encoder, resolver, potentiometer) and a closed-loop controller that drives the error to zero; accurate position, speed and torque control at higher cost and complexity.

3.8 Past Question: Importance of the Actuator Principle

2024 · Q5(a)Discuss why understanding the actuator principle is important when selecting an actuator for a specific application.08Topic: actuator conversion principle

The actuator principle is the physical phenomenon by which input energy is converted into motion (electromagnetic, fluid pressure, piezoelectric, thermal expansion, shape memory …). Different principles determine how an actuator operates and which applications it suits, so understanding the principle is essential because:

  1. It fixes the force/torque, stroke and speed that are physically possible. Hydraulics give very high force density; piezo stacks give nanometre steps but only tens of micrometres of stroke; electric motors give continuous rotation over a wide speed range.
  2. It decides precision and controllability. Electromagnetic actuators are controlled precisely by current and voltage; pneumatic actuators are compressible and suit on–off tasks; thermal and SMA actuators are slow.
  3. It determines the power supply and infrastructure needed (current/voltage, pressure/flow or temperature) and therefore the cost of compressors, pumps or drives.
  4. It reveals dynamic response and bandwidth: piezo (kHz) ≫ electric motor ≫ hydraulic ≫ pneumatic ≫ thermal.
  5. It shows efficiency, heat and noise (losses, cooling, acoustic noise) and therefore energy cost and operator comfort.
  6. It explains environmental limits: sparks from brushed motors in explosive atmospheres, oil leaks in clean rooms, magnetic fields near MRI machines, temperature sensitivity of SMA.
  7. It indicates the failure modes and maintenance (brush wear, seal leakage, fatigue) and the safety behaviour on power loss (spring return, fail-safe).
  8. It allows better design integration: knowing the input quantity tells the designer which power converter, sensor and control strategy go with the actuator.

Example: for a 0–10 µm optical focusing stage a piezoelectric actuator is ideal, while for a 2 m stroke, 50 kN press only hydraulics is practical; neither could be chosen correctly without understanding the principles.

Source lectureKMS · L2 – Actuator and Drive Systems (MTE4107 L2 Actuator and Drive Systems.pptx.pdf, pp. 4–5)

3.9 Past Question: Components of an Actuator System; Stepper vs Servo vs DC Motor

2023 · Q8(d)Shortly describe the components of actuator system. Draw a comparison among stepper, servo and DC motor.10Topic: actuator system; motor comparison

Components of an actuator system (Fig. 3.1): (1) power source – electrical supply, battery, compressor or hydraulic pump; (2) power converter / driver – motor driver, inverter, H-bridge, or proportional valve that meters energy to the actuator according to the controller; (3) actuator – converts that energy into mechanical motion; (4) transmission and mechanical load – gears, belts, screws and the driven mechanism; (5) controller – generates the command so the output follows the set point; (6) sensors – encoders, current or pressure sensors that feed back the actual state.

Principle of controlOpen loop: one pulse → one stepClosed loop with encoder/resolver feedbackSpeed ∝ applied voltage (PWM)
Position accuracyGood (step angle, e.g. 1.8°); errors if steps are lostVery high; error corrected continuouslyPoor without a sensor
Speed rangeLow–medium; torque falls quickly with speedWide, high speedWide, high speed
TorqueHigh at low speed, holding torque at standstillHigh and constant over speed range; high peak torqueDepends on current; good starting torque
Feedback sensorNot neededRequiredNot needed (optional)
Drive / complexityStep driver; simpleServo amplifier + tuned controller; complexSimple H-bridge
Efficiency, heatingDraws current even at rest; runs hotCurrent only as needed; efficientEfficient; brush losses

3.10 Past Question: The Subtractive Approach

2024 · Q6(a)Describe the subtractive actuator selection approach with the help of a suitable example.08Topic: subtractive selection approach

The subtractive approach is a systematic method that starts with the whole set of possible actuator options in a database or catalogue and removes, step by step, those that do not meet the specified application requirements. Instead of choosing one actuator directly, the designer eliminates unfit candidates and narrows the decision space until only viable actuators remain; these are then ranked (weighting method or AHP).

Advantages: no candidate is forgotten (less dependence on habit or supplier bias); works with the incomplete data available early in design; the reason for rejecting each type is recorded; it is quick and needs little actuator expertise, as required for early-phase selection.

Example: actuator for the gripper of a food-packaging robot
Requirements: linear stroke 40 mm, grip force 50 N, open/close in 0.2 s, 107 cycles, washdown environment (IP67, no oil), compressed air available on the line, low cost.
Filter (requirement)RemovedRemaining
Range of motion 40 mm linearpiezo stack, magnetostrictive, thermal (µm strokes)electric, pneumatic, hydraulic, SMA, solenoid
Power supply: air and 24 V DC onlyhydraulic (no pump; oil not allowed)electric, pneumatic, SMA, solenoid
Load 50 N in 0.2 s, 107 cyclesSMA (too slow, fatigue); small solenoid (force falls with stroke)electric linear actuator, pneumatic cylinder
Controllability: open/close only– (both adequate)electric, pneumatic
Environment and cost–electric (sealed), pneumatic
The feasible set {sealed electric gripper, pneumatic cylinder} is then ranked by weighted scoring: with air already available, a stainless pneumatic cylinder is cheapest and simplest, so it is selected.
Source lectureKMS · L2 – Actuator and Drive Systems (MTE4107 L2 Actuator and Drive Systems.pptx.pdf, pp. 9–17) — Approach defined on p. 9; the criteria used as filters on pp. 10–17

3.11 Past Question: Challenges and the Early Design Phase

2024 · Q6(b)What are the challenges faced during actuator selection, and why should actuator selection be carried out during the early design phase?12Topic: challenges; early-phase selection

Challenges in actuator selection

  1. Dependence on experience and intuition: designers often reuse the actuator type they know, so better alternatives are not considered.
  2. Lack of comprehensive design data: catalogues use different formats and omit data (duty cycle, life, dynamic behaviour), so fair comparison is difficult.
  3. Integration complexity: the actuator must fit the mechanics, power supply, drive electronics, sensors and controller at once.
  4. Limited testing and prototyping time: decisions must be made before the actuator can be tried in the real machine.
  5. Supplier bias and incomplete recommendations: vendors promote their own technology.
  6. Cost vs performance trade-offs: the most capable actuator is rarely the cheapest; purchase, energy and maintenance costs all count.
  7. Environmental and operating constraints: temperature, dust, moisture, washdown, explosion risk, noise limits.
  8. Difficulty in standardisation: many sizes, interfaces and protocols, so actuators are hard to standardise across a product range.
  9. Uncertainty in future upgrades: loads, speeds or functions may change later in the product life.
  10. Human and organisational factors: communication gaps between mechanical, electrical and control teams, company preferences, purchasing policy.

Why select the actuator in the early design phase

  • Actuators are among the most expensive and influential components; their cost includes purchase, integration, maintenance and operating (energy) expenses.
  • The rest of the design depends on the actuator: the mechanical structure (mounting, stiffness, transmission), the power supply (air, oil, voltage level, battery size) and the control system (drives, sensors, algorithm). Choosing it late forces redesign of all of these.
  • Early selection, ideally in the layout or conceptual phase, allows important trade-offs to be made while changes are still cheap, and reduces design rework later.
  • It reveals infeasible requirements early (e.g. no actuator meets force and speed within the space).

To be usable this early, the selection procedure must: be quick and simple; need only inputs available early (load, motion range, speed, environment); not require deep actuator knowledge; work with incomplete information; help judge whether trying a new actuator type is worth the time, cost and risk; and balance accuracy with practicality. The subtractive approach followed by weighting/AHP meets these objectives.

Source lectureKMS · L2 – Actuator and Drive Systems (MTE4107 L2 Actuator and Drive Systems.pptx.pdf, pp. 6–8)

Why the consistency ratio is needed. AHP lets the decision maker give intuitive pairwise judgements instead of precise numbers, but a set of judgements may be inconsistent without the decision maker realising it. For example, if Safety is 3× as important as Precision and Precision 2× as important as Maintenance, consistency requires Safety ≈ 6× Maintenance; an entry of 1/2 there would be a contradiction. The consistency ratio measures how far the matrix departs from perfect consistency (λmax=n\lambda_{max}=nλmax​=n), relative to a randomly filled matrix (RI). If CR<0.10CR<0.10CR<0.10 the weights are trustworthy; otherwise the judgements must be revised before the weights are used to rank alternatives.

4. Drive System Design ★★★

Once the actuator type is chosen, it has to be sized and combined with a transmission, power electronics and a controller into a drive system. This chapter covers the second half of the KMS lecture Actuator and Drive Systems and the load calculations that the lecture's design steps require: forces on a vehicle or hoist, torque, power and speed through gears, traction between wheel and ground, and the features of a good drive.

4.1 What a Drive System Is

A drive system is the combination of components that convert energy into controlled motion to move or operate a load. Design of a drive system is the whole process of creating, developing and optimising the components that provide mechanical motion for a vehicle or machine (motor or engine, transmission and control system), including system integration, simulation and testing, so that the drive meets its performance requirements efficiently and reliably.

ComponentFunction
ActuatorConverts electrical, hydraulic or pneumatic energy into rotary or linear motion
Transmission / linkageModifies speed, torque or type of motion to match the load (gears, screws, belts)
Drive / power electronicsSupplies controlled energy to the actuator (motor driver, inverter, pump, valves)
Control systemMakes the motion follow the desired profile precisely (sensors + controller)
Load / environmentThe object being moved and the external conditions that affect performance

4.2 Steps for Designing a Drive System

  1. Define motion requirements: speed, torque or force, stroke, accuracy, environment.
  2. Select the actuator: type and rating (Chapter 3).
  3. Design the transmission / mechanical linkage: adapt actuator torque and speed to the load.
  4. Select the drive / power electronics.
  5. Design the control system so that motion follows the desired trajectory.
  6. Consider traction and load factors, especially for wheeled or mobile systems.
  7. Evaluate and iterate: verify performance and refine.
  8. Integrate all components into a working drive system.

4.3 Load Analysis for a Wheeled Vehicle

The tractive force FtF_tFt​ at the wheels must overcome inertia, grade, rolling resistance and aerodynamic drag (Newton's second law along the slope):

Road-load equation
Ft=ma⏟inertia+mgsin⁡θ⏟grade+Crrmgcos⁡θ⏟rolling+12ρCdAv2⏟aero dragF_t=\underbrace{ma}_{\text{inertia}}+\underbrace{mg\sin\theta}_{\text{grade}}+\underbrace{C_{rr}mg\cos\theta}_{\text{rolling}}+\underbrace{\tfrac12\rho C_dAv^2}_{\text{aero drag}}Ft​=inertiama​​+grademgsinθ​​+rollingCrr​mgcosθ​​+aero drag21​ρCd​Av2​​ Twheel=Ft rw,ωwheel=vrw,Pwheel=Ftv=Twheel ωwheelT_{wheel}=F_t\,r_w,\qquad \omega_{wheel}=\frac{v}{r_w},\qquad P_{wheel}=F_tv=T_{wheel}\,\omega_{wheel}Twheel​=Ft​rw​,ωwheel​=rw​v​,Pwheel​=Ft​v=Twheel​ωwheel​ Tmotor=TwheelG η,ωmotor=G ωwheel,Pmotor=PwheelηT_{motor}=\frac{T_{wheel}}{G\,\eta},\qquad \omega_{motor}=G\,\omega_{wheel},\qquad P_{motor}=\frac{P_{wheel}}{\eta}Tmotor​=GηTwheel​​,ωmotor​=Gωwheel​,Pmotor​=ηPwheel​​ GGG = gear ratio (motor speed ÷ wheel speed), η\etaη = overall efficiency, N=ω×602πN=\omega\times\dfrac{60}{2\pi}N=ω×2π60​ rpm.

Acceleration power. For uniform acceleration from rest to vvv in time ttt, the instantaneous power rises linearly to its peak FtvF_tvFt​v at the end, while the average power equals the energy supplied divided by time: kinetic energy 12mv2\tfrac12mv^221​mv2 plus the work against grade and resistance. The average is used for first sizing because an electric motor can deliver its maximum power over most of the speed range (constant-power region); the peak value shows what a perfectly uniform acceleration would demand.

Unit conversions: 1 mph = 0.44704 m/s; 1 inch = 0.0254 m; g=9.81g=9.81g=9.81 m/s².

4.4 Gear Trains: Torque and Speed

A gear pair with N1N_1N1​ teeth on the input (driver) and N2N_2N2​ on the output has ratio n=N2/N1n=N_2/N_1n=N2​/N1​. Power is conserved apart from losses: Tinωinη=ToutωoutT_{in}\omega_{in}\eta=T_{out}\omega_{out}Tin​ωin​η=Tout​ωout​. Hence a reduction n:1n:1n:1 gives

ωout=ωinn,Tout=n η Tin.\omega_{out}=\frac{\omega_{in}}{n},\qquad T_{out}=n\,\eta\,T_{in}.ωout​=nωin​​,Tout​=nηTin​.

A drum or wheel of radius rrr converts torque to a rope or ground force F=T/rF=T/rF=T/r and speed to v=ωrv=\omega rv=ωr. For servo drives the reflected load inertia is JL/n2J_L/n^2JL​/n2 and the optimum ratio for fastest acceleration is n∗=JL/Jmn^*=\sqrt{J_L/J_m}n∗=JL​/Jm​​ (§1.6).

4.5 Traction and Wheels

A wheel can transmit a tangential force only up to the friction limit: Ft≤μNF_t\le\mu NFt​≤μN, where NNN is the normal load on the driven wheels. If the motor torque exceeds μNr\mu NrμNr the wheel spins. The friction (traction) coefficient depends on the wheel and surface materials and conditions (§4.8). Wheel size affects speed (v=ωrv=\omega rv=ωr), torque (T=FrT=FrT=Fr), ground clearance and the ability to climb obstacles (§4.9).

KEY CHECKPower sets the top-speed and average-acceleration limits; torque × gear ratio sets the low-speed acceleration limit. Both must be checked.
Answer
Select the HPD 40 (750 N·m, 2000 rpm, 120 kW) with ≈ 1:1 direct drive. It is the only motor whose power covers Case I (93.7 kW average for acceleration, 49.9 kW at 100 mph); HPD 35 and HPD 30 are too small. To actually achieve 0–60 mph in 6 s, two HPD 40 units (dual-motor drive, 240 kW, extra mass only 25 kg) are needed. No motor in the datasheet, alone or as a pair, can meet Case II (155 kW average to accelerate and 266 kW to hold 75 mph on a 30° slope); that specification must be relaxed (e.g. 68 mph on 30° with two HPD 40s, or a gentler grade).
Why the answer is not a clean "one motor fits all"
The paper gives no rolling-resistance or drag data, and a 30° slope is far steeper than any road (public roads rarely exceed 15–20 %). Even ignoring all resistance, holding 75 mph on 30° needs mgsin⁡30° v/η=243mg\sin30°\,v/\eta=243mgsin30°v/η=243 kW, twice the largest motor. The examiner most likely expects: compute force, torque, speed and power for each case, compare with the datasheet and choose the HPD 40 as the best available, stating which requirements it cannot meet.

4.8 Past Question: Friction Coefficient of a Robot Wheel

2023 · Q6(a)What factors influence the friction coefficient of a robot's wheel?05Topic: wheel–ground traction

The traction a wheel can develop is Fmax=μNF_{max}=\mu NFmax​=μN, so the friction coefficient μ\muμ decides whether the robot can accelerate, climb and brake without slipping. It depends on:

  1. Wheel material and hardness: soft rubber or polyurethane grips better than hard plastic or metal; harder compounds wear less but slip more.
  2. Tread pattern and surface texture of the tyre: treads clear water and dust and bite into soft ground; smooth tyres give more contact on smooth floors.
  3. Ground surface material and roughness: concrete, tiles, carpet, grass, sand, metal.
  4. Surface condition / contamination: water, oil, dust, ice and loose particles lower μ\muμ sharply.
  5. Normal load and contact pressure: for rubber, μ\muμ falls slightly as pressure rises; weight distribution decides the load on each driven wheel.
  6. Contact area and wheel deformation: width, diameter, inflation pressure and compliance of the tyre.
  7. Slip and speed: μ\muμ rises with small slip, peaks (≈ 10–20 % slip), then falls when the wheel spins; static friction exceeds kinetic friction.
  8. Temperature and wear: rubber properties change with temperature; worn treads lose grip.
Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §4.5, §4.8 of this book); L2 p. 40 only says "consider traction and load factors"

4.9 Past Question: Wheel Size and Obstacle Climbing

2023 · Q6(b)How does the size of a wheel affect a robot's ability to climb over obstacles?10Topic: wheel radius vs step height

Consider a rigid wheel of radius rrr carrying load WWW and pushed horizontally at its axle by force FFF against a step of height hhh (h<rh<rh<r). At the instant of lift-off the wheel loses contact with the floor and pivots about the step edge E. The horizontal distance from the axle to E is a=r2−(r−h)2=2rh−h2a=\sqrt{r^2-(r-h)^2}=\sqrt{2rh-h^2}a=r2−(r−h)2​=2rh−h2​, and the vertical distance is r−hr-hr−h.

Moment balance about E: FFF (lever arm r−hr-hr−h) must overcome WWW (lever arm aaa):

F(r−h)≥W2rh−h2⇒FW≥2rh−h2r−h=2(h/r)−(h/r)21−h/r.F(r-h)\ge W\sqrt{2rh-h^2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{F}{W}\ge\frac{\sqrt{2rh-h^2}}{r-h}=\frac{\sqrt{2(h/r)-(h/r)^2}}{1-h/r}.F(r−h)≥W2rh−h2​⇒WF​≥r−h2rh−h2​​=1−h/r2(h/r)−(h/r)2​​.

The required push depends only on the ratio h/rh/rh/r: it grows steeply as h→rh\to rh→r and becomes infinite at h=rh=rh=r. A larger wheel makes the same step look smaller (h/rh/rh/r smaller), so less force is needed.

KEY IDENTITYPythagoras in the triangle axle–E–vertical: a2+(r−h)2=r2a^2+(r-h)^2=r^2a2+(r−h)2=r2.

Example: step h=20h=20h=20 mm.

  • r=50r=50r=50 mm: F/W=2000−400/30=40/30=1.33F/W=\sqrt{2000-400}/30=40/30=1.33F/W=2000−400​/30=40/30=1.33 – the push must exceed the wheel load.
  • r=100r=100r=100 mm: F/W=4000−400/80=60/80=0.75F/W=\sqrt{4000-400}/80=60/80=0.75F/W=4000−400​/80=60/80=0.75.

Doubling the radius cuts the required push by 44 %. If the push comes from the traction of the other wheels, F≤μWF\le\mu WF≤μW, so climbing is possible only when μ≥2rh−h2/(r−h)\mu\ge\sqrt{2rh-h^2}/(r-h)μ≥2rh−h2​/(r−h), i.e. h≤r(1−1/1+μ2)h\le r\left(1-1/\sqrt{1+\mu^2}\right)h≤r(1−1/1+μ2​); for μ=1\mu=1μ=1, hmax=0.29rh_{max}=0.29rhmax​=0.29r.

INTUITIONA big wheel meets the step edge lower on its circumference, so the contact force points more upward and lifts the wheel instead of just pushing back.

Effects of a larger wheel:

  • ✓ Climbs higher obstacles and crosses gaps and rough ground more easily (rule of thumb: a wheel can climb about r/3r/3r/3 to r/2r/2r/2; never h≥rh\ge rh≥r without special mechanisms).
  • ✓ More ground clearance; rolls more smoothly; lower rolling resistance on soft ground.
  • ✗ Needs more motor torque for the same tractive force (T=FrT=FrT=Fr), or a larger gear ratio.
  • ✗ Higher speed for the same rpm, so coarser speed and position resolution.
  • ✗ Heavier, raises the centre of gravity (tip-over risk), increases robot size.

Designers therefore choose the smallest wheel that clears the largest expected obstacle, or use tracks, rocker-bogie or legged-wheel mechanisms for higher obstacles.

4.10 Past Question: Features of a Good Drive System

2023 · Q6(c)List and describe at least three features that contribute to a good drive system.12Topic: drive system qualities
  1. Adequate torque (force) and speed, matched to the load. The actuator's torque–speed curve, through the transmission ratio, must cover every point of the duty cycle (starting, acceleration, gradients, peak load, top speed) with a margin, without being grossly oversized.
  2. High efficiency. Efficient motor, drive electronics and transmission (low friction gears, belts) reduce energy use, heat and battery size; regenerative braking recovers energy in electric drives.
  3. Good controllability and precision. Smooth, accurate control of position, speed and torque with closed-loop feedback; low backlash and high stiffness in the transmission; fast dynamic response.
  4. Sufficient traction (mobile systems). Proper wheel size, material and load distribution so that the tractive force can be transmitted without slip (§4.8–4.9).
  5. Reliability and durability. Components rated for the duty cycle, temperature and environment (sealing, IP rating), with protection against overload, overcurrent and overheating.
  6. Compactness and low weight. High power density and good packaging, especially in robots and vehicles where mass costs energy and performance.
  7. Safety. Brakes or self-locking for holding loads, emergency stop, fail-safe behaviour on power loss, current limiting.
  8. Low noise and vibration; maintainability and cost. Quiet operation, easy access for service, standard parts, and a reasonable purchase and operating cost.

Each feature should be described with its effect: for example, backlash in a gearbox causes limit cycles in a position loop, so a good positioning drive uses zero-backlash or harmonic gearing and a stiff coupling.

5. Control System Design: Models, Controllers and Stability ★★★

The syllabus item "Control system design: choice of control system, selection and design of controller" is taught in the KMS lecture Control System Design. This chapter collects that material (functions of a control system, factors in choosing one, control algorithms, adaptive control) and adds the classical tools the past papers use: block-diagram modelling and reduction, the second-order step response and the Routh–Hurwitz stability test.

5.1 What a Control System Does

A control system is a set of interconnected components that manage, command, direct or regulate the behaviour of another system so that it produces a desired output, automatically adjusting its inputs to keep stable and optimal performance. Its four functions are:

  • Measurement – sensing the output or process variable (temperature, speed, position, pressure);
  • Comparison – comparing the measured value with the reference (desired) value;
  • Computation – deciding the control action needed to correct the deviation;
  • Correction – applying that action through actuators.

In an open-loop system the output is not measured; the control action is independent of the output (e.g. a toaster timer). In a closed-loop (feedback) system the output is continuously compared with the desired value and deviations are corrected automatically (robots, motion control, thermostats, unmanned vehicles, smart guidance).

5.2 Choosing a Control System

FactorEffect on the choice
Order and dynamic behaviourFirst-order systems are often handled by simple on–off control; second-order systems need proportional-derivative or feedback control; higher-order systems need multi-loop, cascade or state-space control.
LinearityLinear systems are easy to model; saturation, dead zone, backlash and hysteresis need robust or non-linear methods.
Time variationParameters that change with time or load call for adaptive or gain-scheduled control.
Performance specificationsRise time, overshoot, settling time and steady-state error decide which strategy is adequate.
Environment and disturbancesNoise, vibration and uncertainty require disturbance rejection and robustness.
Cost and complexityHardware, software and development cost must be balanced against performance.

5.3 Control Algorithms

The controller processes the error e=r−ye=r-ye=r−y and produces the control signal uuu; it can be built in hardware or in software on a microcontroller, PLC or PC.

ControllerLaw / ideaFeatures and uses
Pu=Kpeu=K_peu=Kp​eSimple, fast; reduces but cannot remove steady-state error. DC motor speed.
PIu=Kpe+Ki∫e dtu=K_pe+K_i\int e\,dtu=Kp​e+Ki​∫edtRemoves steady-state error; slightly slower. Ovens, flow.
PIDu=Kpe+Ki∫e dt+Kddedtu=K_pe+K_i\int e\,dt+K_d\dfrac{de}{dt}u=Kp​e+Ki​∫edt+Kd​dtde​Most widely used; D term predicts and reduces overshoot. Robots, drives, autopilots.
PIDFPID with low-pass filter on the D termSmoother, less noise amplification. Servo systems.
MPCModel predicts future outputs; control optimised over a horizonHandles constraints and multivariable plants. Refineries, autonomous vehicles.
AdaptiveParameters adjusted on-lineTime-varying or uncertain plants (§5.4). Aircraft, manipulators.
Fuzzy logicLinguistic IF–THEN rulesNon-linear, imprecise systems; mimics human reasoning. Washing machines, AC.
Optimal (LQR)Minimises a performance indexEnergy-, time- or error-optimal control (Chapter 6).
State-spaceu=−Kxu=-\mathbf K\mathbf xu=−Kx, with observersMultivariable systems, drones, aircraft.
Bang-bangFully ON or OFF at thresholdsCheap; oscillates. Thermostats, refrigerators.

5.4 Adaptive Control

An adaptive control system has three stages: (1) it starts with controller settings based on an assumed condition; (2) the desired performance is continuously compared with the actual performance; (3) the controller mode and parameters are automatically and continuously adjusted to minimise the difference. Three common forms are gain-scheduled control, self-tuning and model-reference adaptive systems.

Self-tuning control continuously tunes its own parameters by monitoring the controlled variable and the controller output (a parameter estimator identifies the plant on-line). In commercial PID controllers it appears as auto-tuning: at the press of a button the controller injects a small disturbance, measures the response, compares it with the desired one and adjusts the gains by a modified Ziegler–Nichols rule.

5.5 Modelling with Transfer Functions and Block Diagrams

A transfer function G(s)=Y(s)/U(s)G(s)=Y(s)/U(s)G(s)=Y(s)/U(s) is the Laplace transform of the output over that of the input with zero initial conditions. For circuits, element impedances are ZR=RZ_R=RZR​=R, ZL=sLZ_L=sLZL​=sL, ZC=1/(sC)Z_C=1/(sC)ZC​=1/(sC), so V=ZIV=ZIV=ZI in the sss-domain. Each physical law becomes a block; the blocks are joined at summing points (KVL/KCL) and pick-off points.

5.7 Stability and the Routh–Hurwitz Criterion

A linear system is stable if all closed-loop poles (roots of 1+Gc(s)Gp(s)=01+G_c(s)G_p(s)=01+Gc​(s)Gp​(s)=0) lie in the left half of the sss-plane. Routh's test finds how many roots are in the right half-plane without solving the polynomial.

Routh array for a4s4+a3s3+a2s2+a1s+a0a_4s^4+a_3s^3+a_2s^2+a_1s+a_0a4​s4+a3​s3+a2​s2+a1​s+a0​
s4a4a2a0s3a3a10s2b1=a3a2−a4a1a3b2=a0s1c1=b1a1−a3b2b1s0a0\begin{array}{c|ccc}s^4&a_4&a_2&a_0\\s^3&a_3&a_1&0\\s^2&b_1=\dfrac{a_3a_2-a_4a_1}{a_3}&b_2=a_0&\\s^1&c_1=\dfrac{b_1a_1-a_3b_2}{b_1}&&\\s^0&a_0&&\end{array}s4s3s2s1s0​a4​a3​b1​=a3​a3​a2​−a4​a1​​c1​=b1​b1​a1​−a3​b2​​a0​​a2​a1​b2​=a0​​a0​0​ The number of sign changes in the first column = number of right-half-plane roots. Stable ⇔ all first-column entries have the same sign (positive). A row of zeros means roots symmetric about the origin (e.g. on the jωj\omegajω axis: marginal stability).

5.8 Past Question: Requirements of a Control System

2022 · Q6(c)List down the requirements of a control system.05Topic: control-system requirements
  1. Stability: the output must settle for every bounded input and disturbance, with adequate gain and phase margins.
  2. Accuracy: small (ideally zero) steady-state error between output and reference.
  3. Speed of response: short rise and settling times so the output follows the command quickly.
  4. Good damping / limited overshoot: no excessive oscillation (specified %OS).
  5. Disturbance rejection and noise immunity: load changes and sensor noise should have little effect.
  6. Robustness / low sensitivity to parameter variations and model errors.
  7. Reasonable control effort: actuators must not saturate; energy use acceptable.
  8. Reliability, safety, simplicity and cost suited to the application.

These requirements are written as performance specifications (rise time, overshoot, settling time, steady-state error) and must be met by performing the four functions: measurement, comparison, computation and correction.

Source lectureKMS · L3 – Control System Design (MTE4107 L3 Control System design.pptx.pdf, pp. 3–4); L3 – Control System Design (MTE4107 L3 Control System design.pptx.pdf, pp. 21–22)

5.9 Past Question: Gain-Scheduled and Model-Reference Adaptive Control

2022 · Q5(a)Write a short note on Gain Scheduled and Model reference adaptive control.10Topic: adaptive control

Adaptive control adjusts the controller parameters automatically and continuously, so that the desired performance is kept when the plant dynamics or operating conditions change (aircraft at different altitudes and speeds, a robot arm with different payloads, a process at different loads).

Gain-scheduled control

Also called pre-programmed adaptive control. Preset changes in the controller parameters are made on the basis of an auxiliary measurement of some process variable that indicates the operating condition (Fig. 5.2). For each operating condition the gains are designed in advance and stored in a table; the auxiliary measurement selects (or interpolates) the right set. The name comes from early systems in which the only parameter adjusted was the gain KpK_pKp​.

  • Example: aircraft autopilot gains scheduled on dynamic pressure (altitude and Mach number); engine control scheduled on speed and load.
  • Advantage: parameter changes can be made very quickly when conditions change; simple, no on-line identification, easy to verify.
  • Disadvantage: the parameters must be determined for many operating conditions in advance; it is open-loop adaptation, so unforeseen changes are not handled.

Model-reference adaptive control (MRAC/MRAS)

An accurate reference model describing the desired closed-loop behaviour is built. The set value is applied to both the actual system and the model; the difference between the actual output yyy and the model output ymy_mym​ is the error e=ym−ye=y_m-ye=ym​−y, which an adjustment mechanism uses to modify the controller parameters so as to minimise the difference (Fig. 5.4). The adjustment law is usually gradient based (MIT rule dθdt=−γe∂e∂θ\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}=-\gamma e\dfrac{\partial e}{\partial\theta}dtdθ​=−γe∂θ∂e​) or derived from Lyapunov stability theory.

  • Example: a robot joint whose payload changes is made to respond like a chosen second-order model regardless of the payload.
  • Advantage: closed-loop adaptation; the plant is forced to behave like the model even for changes not foreseen.
  • Disadvantage: stability of the adaptation must be guaranteed; adaptation gain must be tuned; needs a sufficiently exciting input.
PointGain-scheduledModel-reference
Adaptation fromAuxiliary measurement of operating conditionError between plant and reference-model outputs
Loop typeOpen-loop adaptation (look-up)Closed-loop adaptation
Speed of changeVery fastLimited by adaptation gain
Design effortDesign gains for many conditionsDesign model and stable adaptation law

6. Compensator Design, Performance Indices and Optimal Control ★★★

"Selection and design of controller" in the syllabus is examined through three tools taught by KMS: the lead and lag compensators (handwritten notes lead lag v3), the performance indices ISE, IAE, ITAE and ITSE (lecture L4), and optimal control with a quadratic index. This chapter derives each tool and solves the 2024 questions.

6.1 Why Compensators?

A step response has a transient part (overshoot, rise and settling time) and a steady-state part (final error). Changing only the gain of a loop usually cannot fix both: raising KKK reduces steady-state error but increases overshoot. A compensator Gc(s)G_c(s)Gc​(s) inserted in series with the plant reshapes the root locus:

  • Lead compensator – improves the transient response (adds phase lead, pulls the locus to the left: faster, better damped).
  • Lag compensator – improves the steady-state response (raises the low-frequency gain, i.e. KvK_vKv​, without disturbing the transient).
  • Lead–lag compensator – both.
Compensator forms (lecture notation)
Lead: Gc(s)=Kcs+1Ts+1αT,  0<α<1\text{Lead: }G_c(s)=K_c\frac{s+\frac1T}{s+\frac1{\alpha T}},\ \ 0<\alpha<1Lead: Gc​(s)=Kc​s+αT1​s+T1​​,  0<α<1 Lag: Gc(s)=Kcs+1Ts+1βT,  β>1\text{Lag: }G_c(s)=K_c\frac{s+\frac1T}{s+\frac1{\beta T}},\ \ \beta>1Lag: Gc​(s)=Kc​s+βT1​s+T1​​,  β>1 zero zc=−1/Tz_c=-1/Tzc​=−1/T, pole pc=−1/(αT)p_c=-1/(\alpha T)pc​=−1/(αT) or −1/(βT)-1/(\beta T)−1/(βT). In a lead network the zero is nearer the origin than the pole; in a lag network the pole is nearer the origin.
Root-locus conditions and error constants
Angle condition: ∠G(sd)=±180°(2k+1)\angle G(s_d)=\pm180°(2k+1)∠G(sd​)=±180°(2k+1). Magnitude condition: ∣G(sd)∣=1|G(s_d)|=1∣G(sd​)∣=1, so K=∏(lengths from poles to sd)∏(lengths from zeros to sd)K=\dfrac{\prod(\text{lengths from poles to }s_d)}{\prod(\text{lengths from zeros to }s_d)}K=∏(lengths from zeros to sd​)∏(lengths from poles to sd​)​.
Velocity error constant Kv=lim⁡s→0sG(s)K_v=\lim_{s\to0}sG(s)Kv​=lims→0​sG(s); steady-state error to a unit ramp ess=1/Kve_{ss}=1/K_vess​=1/Kv​.

6.4 Performance Indices

A performance index is a single number that measures how far the output deviates from the reference over the whole response. It quantifies performance mathematically, allows different controllers to be compared, and turns controller tuning into an optimization problem: choose the parameters that minimise the index (by analytical differentiation, gradient descent, Newton's method or evolutionary algorithms), subject to constraints on parameters or states.

The four integral indices (e(t)=r(t)−y(t)e(t)=r(t)-y(t)e(t)=r(t)−y(t))
ISE=∫0∞e2dt,IAE=∫0∞∣e∣ dt,ITAE=∫0∞t ∣e∣ dt,ITSE=∫0∞t e2dtISE=\int_0^\infty e^2dt,\qquad IAE=\int_0^\infty|e|\,dt,\qquad ITAE=\int_0^\infty t\,|e|\,dt,\qquad ITSE=\int_0^\infty t\,e^2dtISE=∫0∞​e2dt,IAE=∫0∞​∣e∣dt,ITAE=∫0∞​t∣e∣dt,ITSE=∫0∞​te2dt
IndexError treatmentBest forNotes
ISESquared: large errors penalised heavilyMinimising overshoot / large deviationsSensitive to initial conditions; may accept oscillation because long small tails cost little; used in LQR
IAEAbsolute: all errors treated equallyBalanced performance, smooth responseLess sensitive to initial spikes; less prone to oscillation
ITAEAbsolute, weighted by timeQuick settling and small steady-state errorPersistent errors penalised; widely used for PID tuning
ITSESquared, weighted by timeBalance of transient and steady statePenalises both large and persistent errors

Characteristics: indices depend on gains, time constants and delays, so sensitivity analysis shows robustness to parameter changes; disturbance models can be included to measure rejection. Selection depends on the system requirements (settling time, overshoot, steady-state error, control effort), the desired transient (ITAE → quick settling, ISE → small overshoot) and the steady-state specification. Limitations: developed for linear, time-invariant systems; non-linearities (saturation, dead zone, hysteresis) and time-varying parameters need modified indices, linearisation or adaptive control. Indices should be optimised while keeping adequate gain and phase margins.

6.5 Optimal Control with a Quadratic Index

Minimising the error alone can demand infinite actuator effort (for G=K/[s(s+1)]G=K/[s(s+1)]G=K/[s(s+1)], ISE=12+12KISE=\tfrac12+\tfrac1{2K}ISE=21​+2K1​ falls monotonically as K→∞K\to\inftyK→∞). The remedy is to penalise the control signal too:

J=∫0∞{q [r(t)−y(t)]2+u2(t)}dt,q>0 (weight on accuracy relative to effort).J=\int_0^\infty\left\{q\,[r(t)-y(t)]^2+u^2(t)\right\}dt,\qquad q>0\ \text{(weight on accuracy relative to effort)}.J=∫0∞​{q[r(t)−y(t)]2+u2(t)}dt,q>0 (weight on accuracy relative to effort).
Optimal closed loop (spectral factorisation / root-square locus)
For a plant G(s)=N(s)/D(s)G(s)=N(s)/D(s)G(s)=N(s)/D(s) the optimal closed-loop poles are the left-half-plane roots of Δ(s)Δ(−s)=D(s)D(−s)+q N(s)N(−s)=0,\Delta(s)\Delta(-s)=D(s)D(-s)+q\,N(s)N(-s)=0,Δ(s)Δ(−s)=D(s)D(−s)+qN(s)N(−s)=0, and for a type-1 plant with a step reference  Gopt(s)=q N(s)Δ(s)\ G_{opt}(s)=\dfrac{\sqrt q\,N(s)}{\Delta(s)} Gopt​(s)=Δ(s)q​N(s)​, which gives Gopt(0)=1G_{opt}(0)=1Gopt​(0)=1. The same result comes from the LQR (Riccati equation) solution.

6.6 Past Question: Choosing a Performance Index

2024 · Q7(a)For the following systems suggest the most suitable performance index to evaluate the performance of the controller and justify your choice:08Topic: ISE, IAE, ITAE selection
i) Precision positioning requires fast settling time and minimal steady-state error. ii) Crane hoist where a large overshoot is dangerous. iii) Temperature control where a smooth response is preferred.
SystemIndexJustification
(i) Precision positioning – fast settling, minimal steady-state errorITAE ∫t∣e∣dt\int t|e|dt∫t∣e∣dtTime weighting makes errors that persist late in the response expensive, so minimising ITAE drives the system to settle quickly and removes long-term (steady-state) error; the initial unavoidable error is weighted little. It is the standard index for settling-time and accuracy-critical servo tuning.
(ii) Crane hoist – large overshoot dangerousISE ∫e2dt\int e^2dt∫e2dtSquaring penalises large deviations far more than small ones, so a design that minimises ISE avoids large excursions of the load beyond the target (the lecture comparison lists ISE for "minimising overshoot"). ITSE is an alternative if oscillation must also be kept short.
(iii) Temperature control – smooth responseIAE ∫∣e∣dt\int|e|dt∫∣e∣dtAll errors count linearly, so neither the initial error nor small oscillations are over-emphasised; IAE-tuned loops are less oscillatory and give a smooth, balanced response, suitable for a slow thermal process where aggressive correction is not wanted.
Source lectureKMS · L4 – Performance Indices (MTE4107 L4 Performance Indeces.pptx.pdf, pp. 4–8); L4 – Performance Indices (MTE4107 L4 Performance Indeces.pptx.pdf, p. 15)
