7. Real-Time Interfacing: Data Acquisition, I/O and Networks ★★★

The syllabus section "Real time interfacing" covers the elements of data acquisition and control, the I/O process, and networking and communication. The KMS lectures L9 (Data Acquisition and Control), L10 (I/O System) and L11 (Data Communication & Network) are summarised here in full, followed by the past questions.

7.1 Data Acquisition and Control

Data acquisition (DAQ) is the process by which physical phenomena are transformed into electrical signals that are measured and converted into digital form for processing, analysis and storage by a computer. Engineers use DAQ to measure and evaluate real systems, e.g. in automotive testing (frame stress, wind noise, engine vibration, temperature), to optimise prototypes iteratively, and during manufacturing to monitor machines and quality. In most applications the system also acts on the data: control is the process by which digital signals from the system hardware are converted into a form usable by control devices such as actuators and relays, which then control a process. A "DAQ system" therefore usually includes control functions.

The basic elements are: sensors and transducers · field wiring · signal conditioning · DAQ hardware · DAQ software · PC (Fig. 7.1).

7.2 DAQ Hardware and Software

Common types of DAQ hardware: plug-in boards installed in the computer's expansion bus (PCI, PCIe, or external USB modules); stand-alone loggers/controllers that operate independently after setup and communicate by RS-232/RS-485; remote instruments controlled by the computer through the IEEE-488 (GPIB) interface, mainly in laboratories.

  • ADC – converts the analog signal into a digital number (e.g. a thermocouple voltage into a temperature reading). Resolution Q=full-scale range2nQ=\dfrac{\text{full-scale range}}{2^n}Q=2nfull-scale range​: a 12-bit ADC on 0–10 V resolves 10/4096=2.4410/4096=2.4410/4096=2.44 mV.
  • DAC – converts digital commands into analog voltage or current for control (e.g. "50 % speed" → 2.5 V of 5 V to a motor drive).
  • Timing circuitry (clock) – makes the ADC and DAC run at exactly the right rate, so no samples are missed or duplicated (sampling rate at least twice the highest signal frequency; e.g. 44.1 kHz for audio).
  • Bus – conductors that carry data to the computer (PCI, USB, RS-232); on-board FIFO memory buffers data when the bus is busy.
  • Synchronisation – simultaneous sampling (one ADC per channel with a shared clock), RTSI bus to share timing between boards, and PLLs to keep clocks in phase.

DAQ software turns hardware and PC into a complete system. Driver software (from the hardware maker) gives easy access to the hardware without low-level programming. Application software provides analysis, display and control: either a development environment (LabVIEW, MATLAB: the programmer builds a custom application) or configuration-based software with preset functions (LabVIEW DAQ Express, Labtech Notebook). The PC controls the DAQ hardware, collects and stores data, processes it, displays results and sends control signals.

7.3 Transmitting Signals over Long Distances

Field wiring is often the physically largest part of the system and the part most exposed to noise in harsh industrial plants; correct earthing and shielding are essential, and incorrect wiring can make an otherwise good system inaccurate. Over long distances a low-level voltage signal suffers voltage drop in the cable resistance, noise pickup (inductive, capacitive, radio-frequency), ground-potential differences and ground loops, large common-mode voltages, reduced bandwidth from cable capacitance, and exposure to surges and lightning. The two standard cures are the 4–20 mA current loop and digitising near the sensor and transmitting digitally (Figs. 7.3 and 7.4).

7.4 The I/O System

A computer performs I/O (interaction with the outside world through sensors and actuators) and computation. In mechatronic and real-time control systems I/O is often the main task. Devices vary widely in function and speed, so the operating-system kernel contains an I/O subsystem that manages all transfers between CPU and devices and hides device-specific detail behind device drivers, which give a uniform access interface. Two conflicting trends exist: increasing standardisation of interfaces, and an increasingly broad variety of devices.

  • Port – the point of connection of a device; bus – a set of wires shared by several devices with a rigid protocol (PCIe fast bus for graphics, SSDs and DAQ boards; USB/serial slow bus; SAS storage bus); daisy chain – devices connected in series (A → B → C → port), usually operating as a bus.
  • Controller – electronics that operate a port, bus or device: sometimes integrated, sometimes a separate host adapter with its own processor, microcode and memory.

Polling and handshaking. The CPU repeatedly reads the device's status (busy bit) until the device is ready, then transfers the data (programmed I/O). It is simple and works for fast devices or infrequent I/O but wastes CPU cycles on slow devices. Interrupts: the controller asserts the interrupt-request line; after each instruction the CPU checks the line, saves its state, jumps to the interrupt handler, processes the event, restores state and returns. DMA: for large transfers (disks, high-speed DAQ) the CPU writes a command block (source, destination, byte count) and hands the transfer to a DMA controller that moves the data over the memory bus without the CPU; scatter–gather lists allow several transfers in one command.

7.5 Data Communication and Networks

Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices over a transmission medium. Its effectiveness depends on delivery (to the correct destination only), accuracy (no uncorrected alteration), timeliness (real-time delivery) and low jitter (uniform packet delay). The five components are message, sender, receiver, transmission medium and protocol.

TopicKey points
Parallel vs serialParallel: 8/16/32 bits at once on separate wires – fast but costly, short distances. Serial: bit by bit on one line – fewer conductors, cheaper, used for all but the shortest links (e.g. between car microcontrollers).
Asynchronous vs synchronousAsync: independent clocks; each character framed by start and stop bits (less efficient). Sync: common clock; no start/stop bits.
Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplexOne direction only (printer); both directions but one at a time (CB radio); both directions simultaneously (telephone).
NetworkInterconnection of devices able to communicate: hosts and connecting devices (router, switch, modem), joined by wired or wireless media.
TopologiesData bus (all stations on one line; > 100 m between nodes), star (central hub – hub failure stops all), hierarchy/tree (one path between any two stations), ring (popular for LANs, < 100 m, data circulates until removed), mesh (multiple paths).
LAN vs WANLAN: privately owned, one office/building/campus, hosts with addresses, modern LANs use a switch. WAN: town/country/world, interconnects connecting devices, usually run by communication companies and leased.

7.6 Past Question: DAQ Hardware Categories and Long-Distance Problems

2023 · Q8(b)What are the main categories of data acquisition and control hardware? What challenges arise when there are large distances between instrumentation and sensors?07Topic: DAQ hardware; long-distance wiring

Main categories of DAQ and control hardware:

  1. Plug-in I/O boards – installed in the computer's expansion bus (PCI/PCIe) or connected by USB; ADC, DAC, digital I/O and counters on one card; fastest and cheapest per channel, but the sensors must be wired to the PC.
  2. Stand-alone data loggers / controllers – self-contained units with their own processor that log and control independently after configuration and communicate with the host over RS-232/RS-485 (also distributed/remote I/O modules placed near the plant).
  3. Remote (bench) instruments – multimeters, oscilloscopes, analysers controlled from the computer through the IEEE-488 (GPIB) interface, mainly in laboratories.

Challenges of large distances between instrumentation and sensors:

  • Signal attenuation: the cable resistance causes voltage drop, so a millivolt signal arriving at the DAQ is smaller than at the sensor.
  • Electrical noise pickup: long wires act as antennas for magnetic, capacitive and radio interference from motors, drives and power cables.
  • Ground loops and ground-potential differences: the earth at the sensor and at the computer differ by volts, causing offset errors, hum and even damage.
  • Common-mode voltage beyond the input range of the DAQ hardware.
  • Bandwidth loss and reflections from cable capacitance and inductance.
  • Safety and protection: surges and lightning on long outdoor runs; need for isolation.
  • Cost and maintenance of long multi-core screened cabling; difficulty of troubleshooting.
Source lectureKMS · L9 – Data Acquisition and Control (MTE4107 L9 Data Acquisition and Control.pdf, p. 11); L9 – Data Acquisition and Control (MTE4107 L9 Data Acquisition and Control.pdf, p. 7) — Long-distance problems only outlined under field wiring — see §7.3

7.7 Past Question: Two Methods for Signal Integrity over Long Distances

2023 · Q8(c)Describe the two methods for maintaining signal integrity over long distances in data acquisition systems.10Topic: current loop; remote digital transmission

Method 1 — Current-loop transmission (4–20 mA)

The sensor signal is converted at the sensor by a transmitter into a current between 4 and 20 mA proportional to the measured range (Fig. 7.3). A loop supply (typically 24 V DC) drives the current round the loop; at the DAQ end a precision resistor (250 Ω) converts it back into 1–5 V for the ADC.

  • In a series loop the same current flows everywhere, so cable resistance and voltage drop do not change the reading (as long as the supply has enough compliance voltage).
  • A current source has a high output impedance and the receiver a low impedance, so induced noise voltages produce very little error; twisted pair cancels magnetic pickup.
  • Live zero: 4 mA represents 0 %, so 0 mA means a broken wire or failed transmitter – a built-in fault check; the 4 mA also powers two-wire transmitters over the same pair.
  • Works reliably over hundreds of metres to about 1 km; standard for industrial instruments (HART adds digital data on the same pair).

Method 2 — Digitise at the sensor and transmit digitally (remote / distributed DAQ)

The signal conditioning and the ADC are placed in a remote I/O module or smart transmitter close to the sensors, so the analog path is very short. The digitised data are sent to the host over a digital serial link – RS-485 (differential, up to about 1200 m), a fieldbus (Profibus, Modbus, CAN, Foundation Fieldbus), industrial Ethernet, or optical fibre for kilometres and total immunity to EMI (Fig. 7.4).

  • Digital levels have a large noise margin: the receiver only has to tell 0 from 1, so moderate noise causes no error.
  • Error detection (parity, CRC checksums) and retransmission ensure accuracy; differential signalling rejects common-mode noise.
  • One twisted pair carries many channels (multi-drop), reducing cabling cost; isolation between modules breaks ground loops.
Good practice with either method
Amplify the signal close to the sensor (raise it above the noise before the long run), use shielded twisted-pair cable with the shield earthed at one end only, use differential inputs and isolation amplifiers, keep signal cables away from power cables, and add surge protection on outdoor runs.
Source lectureKMS · L9 – Data Acquisition and Control (MTE4107 L9 Data Acquisition and Control.pdf, p. 7) — Only the need for earthing and shielding is given; the two methods — see §7.3, §7.7

7.8 Past Question: Components of a DAQ System

2024 · Q8(c)Explain the function of each component of a DAQ system with the help of the functional block diagram.15Topic: elements of a DAQ system

Draw Fig. 7.1 (physical phenomena → transducers → field wiring → signal conditioning → DAQ hardware → PC with software, and the output path back to actuators). The function of each component:

  1. Physical phenomenon: the quantity to be measured – temperature, pressure, light intensity, force, motion.
  2. Transducers and sensors: the interface between the real world and the DAQ system; they convert the physical phenomenon into a measurable electrical signal (voltage, current, resistance change) that the conditioning or DAQ hardware can accept (thermocouple, strain gauge, RTD, accelerometer). The range of phenomena a system can measure depends on its transducers.
  3. Field wiring and communications cabling: the physical connection from the transducers to the signal conditioning/DAQ hardware, and from remote hardware to the host computer. Often the largest part of the system and the most exposed to noise, so correct earthing and shielding are vital.
  4. Signal conditioning: converts the transducer signal into a form acceptable to the DAQ hardware, especially the ADC:
    • filtering – low-pass filters remove high-frequency noise from mV signals;
    • amplification – raises the signal to the ADC input range, maximising resolution; the amplifier is placed close to the sensor;
    • linearisation – corrects non-linear sensors (thermocouples, thermistors) in hardware or software;
    • isolation – protects the computer from high-voltage spikes and faults, ensures operator safety, prevents noise coupling between channels;
    • excitation – supplies the precise voltage or current needed by strain gauges, RTDs and thermistors.
  5. DAQ hardware: the core of the system that converts, processes and transfers data between sensors and computer (plug-in board, stand-alone logger, or GPIB instrument). Its parts: ADC (analog → digital for measurement), DAC (digital → analog for control and signal generation), timing circuitry (precise sample rate), bus interface with on-board memory (PCI, USB, RS-232), and synchronisation (shared clock, RTSI, PLL) so that all channels are aligned in time.
  6. DAQ software: driver software gives easy access to the hardware; application software (LabVIEW, MATLAB, or configuration-based packages) provides acquisition, analysis, display, logging and control.
  7. PC (host computer): controls the DAQ hardware (when and how measurements are taken), collects and stores data, processes and analyses it, displays results as graphs, tables or dashboards, and sends control signals back.
  8. Control outputs and actuators: the DAC and digital outputs drive actuators, relays and valves that act on the process, closing the loop.
Example to quote
Monitoring an engine on a test bed: a thermocouple (transducer) produces a few mV; shielded cable (field wiring) carries it to an amplifier, 10 Hz low-pass filter and cold-junction compensation (signal conditioning); a 16-bit USB DAQ module samples it at 10 S/s (DAQ hardware); LabVIEW (software) on the PC plots temperature, stores it, and through a DAC output reduces the throttle if the limit is exceeded.
Source lectureKMS · L9 – Data Acquisition and Control (MTE4107 L9 Data Acquisition and Control.pdf, pp. 4–16)

7.9 Past Question: How the Processor Commands an I/O Controller

2024 · Q8(d)How does the processor give commands and data to a controller to accomplish an I/O transfer?06Topic: device registers, port-mapped and memory-mapped I/O

The device controller has one or more registers for data and control signals; the processor communicates with the controller by reading and writing bit patterns in these registers (Fig. 7.5). Typically there are four:

  • data-in register – read by the host to get input;
  • data-out register – written by the host to send output;
  • status register – bits read by the host: command completed, byte available in data-in, device error, busy;
  • control register – written by the host to start a command or change the device mode.

The registers are reached in one of two ways:

  1. Port-mapped (isolated) I/O: special I/O instructions (e.g. IN/OUT) transfer a byte or word to an I/O port address; the instruction drives the bus lines to select the device and move bits into or out of a device register (e.g. ports 3F8–3FF for the primary serial port on a PC).
  2. Memory-mapped I/O: the device-control registers are mapped into the processor's address space; the CPU uses ordinary load/store (data-transfer) instructions at those memory locations.

Handshaking (polling) sequence for an output byte: (1) host reads the busy bit until clear; (2) host sets the write bit in the command register and writes the byte to data-out; (3) host sets command-ready; (4) controller sees command-ready and sets busy; (5) controller reads the command and data-out and performs the I/O; (6) controller clears command-ready, clears the error bit and clears busy. Instead of polling, the controller may raise an interrupt when ready, or a DMA controller may move large blocks directly to memory.

Source lectureKMS · L10 – I/O System (MTE4107 L10 IO.pdf, pp. 10–11); L10 – I/O System (MTE4107 L10 IO.pdf, pp. 13–15)

7.10 Past Question: Why Access Control Is Needed in Control Networks

2024 · Q8(b)Briefly explain why access control methods are required in control networks.06Topic: network access control

In a network many stations share one transmission medium (a bus or ring). If two stations transmit at the same time their signals collide and both messages are corrupted. Access control methods are necessary to ensure that only one user of the network transmits at any one time. In a control network this also makes communication orderly, fair and predictable, so that time-critical sensor data and actuator commands arrive within their deadlines (deterministic timing), bandwidth is not wasted on collisions and retransmissions, and no station monopolises the medium.

  • Token passing (rings): a special bit pattern, the token, circulates; a station may transmit only when it holds the token, attaching it to the end of its data; the next station wishing to send removes the token and attaches it to its own data. Collision-free and deterministic.
  • Slot passing (rings): empty slots circulate; a station deposits its data in the first empty slot.
  • CSMA/CD (bus/tree, Ethernet): stations listen before transmitting (carrier sense); any station may gain access (multiple access); if two start together the collision is detected, both stop and retry after a random time.

Fieldbuses such as CAN use non-destructive bitwise arbitration (priority by message identifier) for the same purpose.

Source lectureKMS · L11 – Data Communication & Network (MTE4107 L11 Data Communication & Network.pdf, pp. 20–21)

8. Intelligent Systems: Kalman Filtering and Machine Learning ★★★

The syllabus asks for "design and implementation of a prototype in artificial intelligence". The past papers examine two parts of it: state estimation with the Kalman filter (2023 Q7, 35 marks) and the use of machine learning in mechatronic systems (2022 Q8(c)). Neither is in the KMS slide decks, so this chapter builds both from standard theory, step by step.

8.1 The Estimation Problem in Robotics

A robot never knows its state (position, heading, velocity) exactly. Dead reckoning from wheel encoders (odometry) is smooth but drifts, because wheel slip and small errors accumulate without bound. Absolute sensors (GPS, camera, compass, landmarks) do not drift but are noisy, slow or occasionally missing. The best estimate combines both, weighting each by how much it can be trusted. The Kalman filter does this optimally for linear systems with Gaussian noise.

8.2 The Kalman Filter Equations

Model
xk=Axk−1+Buk+wk,wk∼N(0,Q)(process / motion model)\mathbf x_k=\mathbf A\mathbf x_{k-1}+\mathbf B\mathbf u_k+\mathbf w_k,\quad \mathbf w_k\sim N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf Q)\qquad\text{(process / motion model)}xk​=Axk−1​+Buk​+wk​,wk​∼N(0,Q)(process / motion model) zk=Hxk+vk,vk∼N(0,R)(measurement model)\mathbf z_k=\mathbf H\mathbf x_k+\mathbf v_k,\quad \mathbf v_k\sim N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf R)\qquad\text{(measurement model)}zk​=Hxk​+vk​,vk​∼N(0,R)(measurement model) x\mathbf xx state, u\mathbf uu known input, z\mathbf zz measurement, Q\mathbf QQ process-noise covariance, R\mathbf RR measurement-noise covariance, P\mathbf PP estimate covariance.
Predict – update cycle
Predict:  x^k−=Ax^k−1+Buk,Pk−=APk−1AT+Q\ \hat{\mathbf x}_k^-=\mathbf A\hat{\mathbf x}_{k-1}+\mathbf B\mathbf u_k,\qquad \mathbf P_k^-=\mathbf A\mathbf P_{k-1}\mathbf A^T+\mathbf Q x^k−​=Ax^k−1​+Buk​,Pk−​=APk−1​AT+Q

Derivation of the gain (scalar case)

Let the prediction be x^−\hat x^-x^− with error variance P−P^-P−, and the measurement z=x+vz=x+vz=x+v with variance RRR (independent errors). Form the blend x^=x^−+K(z−x^−)=(1−K)x^−+Kz\hat x=\hat x^-+K(z-\hat x^-)=(1-K)\hat x^-+Kzx^=x^−+K(z−x^−)=(1−K)x^−+Kz. Its error is e=(1−K)e−+Kve=(1-K)e^-+Kve=(1−K)e−+Kv, so

P=E[e2]=(1−K)2P−+K2R.P=E[e^2]=(1-K)^2P^-+K^2R.P=E[e2]=(1−K)2P−+K2R.

Minimise with respect to KKK: dPdK=−2(1−K)P−+2KR=0\dfrac{dP}{dK}=-2(1-K)P^-+2KR=0dKdP​=−2(1−K)P−+2KR=0 ⇒

K=P−P−+R,P=(1−K)P−=P−RP−+R.K=\frac{P^-}{P^-+R},\qquad P=(1-K)P^-=\frac{P^-R}{P^-+R}.K=P−+RP−​,P=(1−K)P−=P−+RP−R​.

The matrix form follows in the same way by minimising the trace of P\mathbf PP.

KEY RESULTP<min⁡(P−,R)P<\min(P^-,R)P<min(P−,R): the fused estimate is better than either source alone.

INTUITIONThe gain is the fraction of the prediction's uncertainty in the total uncertainty.

Non-linear systems. For a robot, xk=f(xk−1,uk)\mathbf x_k=f(\mathbf x_{k-1},\mathbf u_k)xk​=f(xk−1​,uk​) and zk=h(xk)\mathbf z_k=h(\mathbf x_k)zk​=h(xk​) are non-linear (sines and cosines of heading). The Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) uses fff and hhh for the predicted state and measurement, and their Jacobians F=∂f/∂x\mathbf F=\partial f/\partial\mathbf xF=∂f/∂x and H=∂h/∂x\mathbf H=\partial h/\partial\mathbf xH=∂h/∂x in place of A\mathbf AA and H\mathbf HH in the covariance equations. (The Unscented KF and particle filter are alternatives for strongly non-linear cases.)

8.3 Machine Learning in Brief

Machine learning (ML) lets a system learn a mapping or a policy from data instead of having it programmed explicitly. Supervised learning learns from labelled examples (classification: which gesture? regression: what force?) using linear models, SVM, decision trees, random forests and neural networks (CNNs for images, RNN/LSTM for time series). Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering, anomaly detection, dimensionality reduction such as PCA). Reinforcement learning learns a control policy by trial and reward. ML models are trained offline on logged data, validated on separate data, then deployed on the embedded controller or an edge computer.

8.4 Past Question: What a Kalman Filter Is and Why Robots Need It

2023 · Q7(a)What is a Kalman filter and why are they required in robotics?05Topic: Kalman filter – definition and purpose

A Kalman filter is a recursive optimal state estimator. It combines a mathematical model of how a system evolves (prediction) with noisy sensor measurements (correction) to produce, at every time step, the minimum-variance estimate of the system state together with its uncertainty (covariance). It is optimal for linear systems with Gaussian noise and is extended to non-linear systems as the EKF/UKF.

Why robots need it:

  • Every sensor is noisy (encoders, IMU, GPS, cameras, ultrasonic), and raw readings would make control jittery.
  • Odometry drifts (wheel slip, gyro bias) while absolute sensors are noisy or slow; sensor fusion by the KF gives an estimate better than any single sensor.
  • Some states cannot be measured directly (velocity, heading, gyro bias); the KF estimates them from the model.
  • It works recursively in real time with little memory and computation – suitable for microcontrollers.
  • It provides the uncertainty of the estimate, used for localisation, SLAM, navigation, tracking of objects and robust control.
Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §8.1–8.2 of this book)

8.5 Past Question: How the Kalman Gain Balances Prediction and Measurement

2023 · Q7(b)How does the Kalman gain balance between prediction and measurement in the Kalman filter?07Topic: Kalman gain

The update is a weighted blend: x^=x^−+K(z−Hx^−)\hat x=\hat x^-+K(z-H\hat x^-)x^=x^−+K(z−Hx^−). The innovation z−Hx^−z-H\hat x^-z−Hx^− is the disagreement between the measurement and the prediction, and the Kalman gain KKK decides how much of it is accepted. In the matrix form K=P−HT(HP−HT+R)−1\mathbf K=\mathbf P^-\mathbf H^T(\mathbf H\mathbf P^-\mathbf H^T+\mathbf R)^{-1}K=P−HT(HP−HT+R)−1; in the scalar case with H=1H=1H=1,

K=P−P−+R,0≤K≤1,x^=(1−K) x^−+K z.K=\frac{P^-}{P^-+R},\qquad 0\le K\le1,\qquad \hat x=(1-K)\,\hat x^-+K\,z.K=P−+RP−​,0≤K≤1,x^=(1−K)x^−+Kz.
  • Measurement very accurate (R→0R\to0R→0): K→1K\to1K→1, x^→z\hat x\to zx^→z – the filter trusts the sensor.
  • Prediction very accurate (P−→0P^-\to0P−→0, or sensor very noisy R→∞R\to\inftyR→∞): K→0K\to0K→0, x^→x^−\hat x\to\hat x^-x^→x^− – the filter trusts the model and ignores the noisy reading.
  • In between, each source is weighted inversely to its variance: x^=R x^−+P−zP−+R\hat x=\dfrac{R\,\hat x^-+P^-z}{P^-+R}x^=P−+RRx^−+P−z​.

Numerical illustration. Prediction x^−=10.0\hat x^-=10.0x^−=10.0 m with P−=4P^-=4P−=4 m²; measurement z=10.6z=10.6z=10.6 m with R=1R=1R=1 m². Then K=4/(4+1)=0.8K=4/(4+1)=0.8K=4/(4+1)=0.8, x^=10.0+0.8(0.6)=10.48\hat x=10.0+0.8(0.6)=10.48x^=10.0+0.8(0.6)=10.48 m, P=(1−0.8)4=0.8P=(1-0.8)4=0.8P=(1−0.8)4=0.8 m² – smaller than both 4 and 1. If instead P−=1P^-=1P−=1, R=4R=4R=4: K=0.2K=0.2K=0.2 and the estimate stays near the prediction.

INTUITIONQ\mathbf QQ (process noise) inflates P−P^-P− at every prediction, so a large Q\mathbf QQ keeps the gain high and the filter responsive; a large R\mathbf RR keeps it low and the estimate smooth. Tuning Q\mathbf QQ and R\mathbf RR sets this balance.

Because PPP shrinks after each update and grows by QQQ at each prediction, the gain adapts automatically: it is large at start-up (initial estimate uncertain) and settles to a steady value (Fig. 8.2).

8.6 Past Question: The Covariance Matrix

2023 · Q7(c)What is covariance matrix, and what does it represent in the context of a Kalman filter?05Topic: covariance matrices P, Q, R

For a random vector x\mathbf xx with mean xˉ\bar{\mathbf x}xˉ, the covariance matrix is Σ=E[(x−xˉ)(x−xˉ)T]\mathbf\Sigma=E[(\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x})(\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x})^T]Σ=E[(x−xˉ)(x−xˉ)T]. It is square, symmetric and positive semi-definite. Its diagonal elements are the variances σi2\sigma_i^2σi2​ of each component (spread, uncertainty), and the off-diagonal elements are the covariances σij\sigma_{ij}σij​, which show how two components vary together (correlation ρij=σij/σiσj\rho_{ij}=\sigma_{ij}/\sigma_i\sigma_jρij​=σij​/σi​σj​). For a 2-D position, it describes an uncertainty ellipse.

In the Kalman filter there are three:

  • P\mathbf PP – state-estimate covariance: how uncertain the current estimate is. E.g. for [x,y,θ][x,y,\theta][x,y,θ], P11=0.01P_{11}=0.01P11​=0.01 m² means σx=0.1\sigma_x=0.1σx​=0.1 m; a non-zero P23P_{23}P23​ means errors in yyy and θ\thetaθ are correlated (a heading error produces a sideways position error).
  • Q\mathbf QQ – process-noise covariance: uncertainty of the motion model (wheel slip, unmodelled dynamics).
  • R\mathbf RR – measurement-noise covariance: accuracy of the sensors (from datasheets or calibration).

P\mathbf PP grows in the predict step (APAT+Q\mathbf A\mathbf P\mathbf A^T+\mathbf QAPAT+Q), shrinks in the update step, and through K\mathbf KK decides how strongly each measurement corrects each state.

8.8 Past Question: Machine Learning for Control and Decision Making

2022 · Q8(c)How can machine learning algorithm be applied in mechatronic systems for enhancing control and decision-making process?10Topic: ML in mechatronic systems

ML adds the ability to learn from data where a precise physical model is hard to obtain or the environment changes. Main applications:

  1. Perception and sensor interpretation: CNNs detect and classify objects, obstacles, lanes and defects from cameras and LiDAR; classifiers (LDA, SVM, neural networks) recognise gestures from EMG signals in a prosthetic hand; ML fuses multiple sensors into a reliable state.
  2. System identification and modelling: neural networks or Gaussian processes learn non-linear plant dynamics (friction, backlash, aerodynamic effects) from input–output data; the learned model is used in model-predictive control or feed-forward compensation.
  3. Adaptive and intelligent control: ML tunes PID gains on-line, adjusts to payload or wear (learning-based adaptive control), neural-network and fuzzy-neural controllers handle non-linear plants; reinforcement learning learns control policies by trial and reward (walking robots, drone flight, robotic grasping).
  4. Decision making and planning: path planning and obstacle avoidance for autonomous robots and vehicles; behaviour selection; scheduling of manufacturing cells.
  5. Predictive maintenance and fault diagnosis: ML on vibration, current and temperature data detects anomalies and predicts failures (e.g. rolling-bearing faults) before they stop the machine.
  6. Quality control and optimisation: vision-based inspection; optimisation of process parameters (welding current, feed rate) from historical data; energy optimisation.
  7. Human–machine interaction: speech and gesture recognition, intention estimation in exoskeletons and prostheses.

Implementation: collect and label data → pre-process and extract features → train and validate the model → deploy on the embedded processor or edge computer (quantised models, TinyML) → monitor and re-train. Challenges: need for large, representative data; real-time computation on limited hardware; safety and explainability of learned controllers; robustness to conditions not seen in training. ML therefore usually complements classical control (e.g. ML perception + PID/MPC actuation) rather than replacing it.

Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §8.3, §8.8 of this book)

9. Case Study: Myoelectrically Controlled Prosthetic Arm ★★★

The 2022 paper set a whole question group on the myoelectric prosthetic arm, a classic mechatronic case study that draws on every chapter of this book: requirement definition and design process (Ch. 1), EMG sensing and signal conditioning (Ch. 2), actuator selection (Ch. 3), drive design (Ch. 4), control (Ch. 5) and machine learning (Ch. 8). The material is not on the KMS slides; it is built from standard biomedical-mechatronics practice.

9.1 Upper-Limb Prostheses

TypeHow it worksPros / cons
Passive (cosmetic)Shaped and coloured like a hand; no active motion (some have manually positioned joints)Light, cheap, natural look / no function
Body-poweredA harness and Bowden cable transmit shoulder motion to open/close a hook or handRobust, cheap, gives force feedback / harness discomfort, limited grip force, unnatural motion
Externally powered – myoelectricEMG electrodes in the socket detect muscle activity; a controller drives electric motors in the hand, wrist or elbowNo harness, natural intuitive control, strong grip / heavier, expensive, needs battery and training
Hybride.g. body-powered elbow + myoelectric handCombines advantages for high-level amputees

Amputation levels: partial hand, wrist disarticulation, transradial (below elbow, the most common for myoelectric hands), elbow disarticulation, transhumeral (above elbow), shoulder disarticulation. Higher levels need more powered joints and have fewer control muscles available.

Myoelectric control strategies: (1) on/off (threshold) – flexor EMG above threshold closes, extensor opens; (2) proportional – speed or force proportional to the EMG envelope; (3) mode switching by co-contraction to select wrist or elbow; (4) pattern recognition – features from several channels are classified (LDA, SVM, ANN) into gestures; (5) targeted muscle reinnervation – nerves re-routed to chest muscles to create new EMG sites.

9.2 Prosthetic Hand and Arm Mechanisms

MechanismDescriptionCharacteristics
Single-DOF gripper / split hookOne motor opens and closes a hook or a three-jaw chuck (thumb + two fingers) through gearsSimple, robust, strong, light; only one grasp type
Linkage-driven fingersEach finger is a four-bar or crossed linkage; one actuator flexes all its joints in a fixed ratioStiff, durable, accurate, easy to 3D-print; fixed finger trajectory
Tendon (cable)-drivenCables run like tendons through the finger and are pulled by a motor/spool; springs or elastic bands extendLight, anthropomorphic, easy to make underactuated; cable stretch, friction, maintenance
Underactuated (adaptive)Fewer actuators than joints; differential (whiffle-tree, springs) lets fingers wrap round objectsAdaptive grasp with few motors; less individual control
Gear / worm-gear driven jointsA motor at each joint, often with a non-back-drivable worm gearHolds grip without power; heavier, more motors
Multi-articulating hand5–6 motors: each finger plus thumb rotationMany grasp patterns (power, precision, lateral, tripod); expensive, complex control
Soft / fluidic actuatorsPneumatic or hydraulic soft fingersCompliant, safe; needs pump/valves, less force
Wrist and elbowWrist rotator (motor + gearbox), powered elbow (lead screw or harmonic drive)Needed for higher amputation levels

9.3 Past Question: Why the Prosthetic Arm Is a Mechatronic System

2022 · Q7(a)“Myo electrically controlled prosthetic arm is a mechatronic system.” Justify the statement.10Topic: prosthetic arm as a mechatronic system

A mechatronic system is the synergistic integration of mechanical engineering, electronics, sensors, actuators, control and software, designed concurrently to perform an intelligent function. A myoelectric arm contains all of these, and none of them works alone (Fig. 9.1):

Mechatronic elementIn the myoelectric arm
Mechanical systemFingers, linkages or tendons, joints, gears, wrist and elbow mechanisms, socket and frame (3D-printed or composite), designed for weight, strength and grasp geometry
SensorsSurface EMG electrodes (user intent); force/pressure sensors in fingertips; joint position encoders or potentiometers; motor current sensing; sometimes IMU
Signal conditioning / electronicsInstrumentation amplifiers, band-pass and notch filters, rectifier and envelope detector, ADC; motor drivers (H-bridges, PWM)
ActuatorsDC micro gear-motors, servo motors or linear actuators that move the fingers, wrist and elbow
Controller and softwareMicrocontroller running feature extraction, gesture classification (threshold, LDA, neural network), proportional speed/force control, closed-loop grip control, safety logic
PowerRechargeable Li-ion battery with regulation and protection
Human–machine interfaceThe user's muscles are the "input device"; vibrotactile feedback or LEDs return information

Mechatronic operation: the user contracts a muscle → electrodes sense the EMG → electronics condition it → the microcontroller decides the intended movement and computes the command → drivers and motors actuate the mechanism → force and position sensors feed back so that the grip is controlled and objects are not crushed. The design is integrated: the mechanism determines motor torque and battery size, the motor and electrode placement determine noise and signal processing, and the control software compensates for mechanical limits. This closed sense–process–actuate loop with concurrent multi-domain design is exactly the definition of a mechatronic system, so the statement is justified.

Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §9.1–9.2 of this book)

9.4 Past Question: Types of Prosthetic Arm Mechanisms and a Feasible Choice

2022 · Q7(b)What are the different types of prosthetic arm mechanisms? What type of mechanism is deemed feasible to develop by you and why?08Topic: prosthetic mechanisms; design choice

Types (§9.1–9.2): by power source – passive, body-powered (cable and harness), externally powered (myoelectric), hybrid; by hand mechanism – single-DOF gripper/split hook, linkage-driven fingers, tendon/cable-driven fingers, underactuated adaptive hands, gear/worm-gear driven joints, multi-articulating hands, and soft fluidic hands; plus powered wrist rotators and elbows.

Feasible choice for a student/low-cost design: a 3D-printed, underactuated, linkage- (or tendon-) driven transradial hand with myoelectric control – each finger flexed by one small DC micro gear-motor (or the four fingers by two motors), the thumb by one motor, and a worm or high-ratio gear so the grip holds without power.

Reasons:

  1. Low cost and available technology: PLA/nylon printing, hobby micro gear-motors, open-source EMG sensors and microcontrollers.
  2. Light weight (target < 500 g for the hand): few motors and printed parts.
  3. Adaptive grasp with few actuators: underactuation lets fingers wrap around objects of different shapes, giving power and cylindrical grips without complex control.
  4. Simple control: two EMG channels (flexor/extensor) with threshold or proportional control are enough; pattern recognition can be added later.
  5. Robustness and maintainability: linkages do not stretch like cables; broken parts can be reprinted.
  6. Safety and user comfort: no harness; grip force limited by motor current sensing.

A fully multi-articulating hand is more dexterous but far more expensive, heavier and harder to control; a body-powered hook is cheap but uncomfortable and not "intelligent".

Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §9.2 of this book)

9.5 Past Question: Multiple Sensors for Finger Gesture Detection

2022 · Q7(d)What potential advantages could be gained by using multiple sensors instead of a single sensor for individual finger gesture detection?04Topic: multi-channel EMG
  • More information / higher accuracy: different finger movements activate different muscles (or parts of a muscle); several channels capture the spatial pattern, so a classifier can separate individual-finger gestures that a single channel cannot.
  • More gestures and simultaneous/proportional control of several fingers.
  • Robustness and redundancy: if one electrode shifts, loses contact, or is affected by sweat, noise or fatigue, the others still carry the information.
  • Crosstalk handling and noise reduction: comparing channels separates the activity of neighbouring muscles; averaging or fusion reduces random noise; fusion with other sensors (IMU, force-myography) further improves reliability.
Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §9.1, §2.7 of this book)

9.6 Past Question: Steps to Develop a Myoelectric Prosthetic Arm

2022 · Q8(a)Write down the steps to develop a myo-electrically controlled prosthetic arm from the beginning.10Topic: development process of a prosthetic arm
  1. Need recognition and user assessment: amputation level, residual-limb condition, available EMG sites, daily tasks, user goals; consult clinicians.
  2. Requirements specification: degrees of freedom, grip types, grip force (e.g. 30–60 N), finger closing time (≈ 1 s), mass (< 500 g hand), size matching the sound hand, battery life (a full day), noise, cost, safety and comfort.
  3. Literature and concept study: review existing prostheses; generate concepts (mechanism type, actuator, control strategy) and select the best by a weighted decision matrix.
  4. Mechanical design: CAD of fingers, thumb, palm, wrist and socket; kinematic and force analysis of the mechanism; material selection; stress check.
  5. Actuator and drive selection: size the motors and gear ratios from the grip force and speed; select motor drivers (Ch. 3–4).
  6. Sensing and signal conditioning: choose electrodes and their placement; design the EMG amplifier, filters, rectifier and envelope detector; add force and position sensors (Ch. 2).
  7. Controller and software: select the microcontroller; write firmware for data acquisition, feature extraction (MAV, RMS), classification or threshold control, proportional and closed-loop grip control, and safety limits; collect training data and train the classifier.
  8. Power system: battery, charging, regulation, protection, power management (sleep modes).
  9. Prototyping and integration: 3D-print the parts, assemble mechanics, electronics and software; build the socket; integrate wiring and battery.
  10. Testing and validation: bench tests (force, speed, endurance, current), EMG classification accuracy, then tests with the user (functional tests such as box-and-block, comfort, fatigue).
  11. User training, refinement and documentation: train the user, iterate the design, document drawings, circuits and code; address safety standards and medical-device approval before clinical use.
Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §9.6, §1.2 of this book)
